OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre Changelog Deep Analysis

Overview

The OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre pre-release version focuses on three core directions:

  1. Capability Expansion: Memory, UI, video generation, plugin declarations, etc.
  2. Integration Usability: Experience enhancements for existing integrations like Feishu, Teams, Ollama, OpenAI-compatible
  3. Stability Fixes: Critical path fixes for Codex OAuth, audio transcription, Talk Mode, WhatsApp, ACP streaming output

Overall, this release is not about single major features but continuous convergence around “stronger multimodal interaction, clearer integration boundaries, and reduced internal leakage and configuration friction.”

Key Highlights:

  • 9 feature enhancements covering Dreaming, WebChat, video generation, plugin setup, Teams/Feishu, etc.
  • 12 fixes focusing on Codex OAuth, audio transcription, Talk Mode, ACP/QA leakage control, WhatsApp path consistency
  • Continuation of 2026.4.10 directions in Codex, Active Memory, strict agentic execution, provider classification, and QA systems

Deep Dive into New Features

Dreaming/memory-wiki: ChatGPT Import Integration + Imported Insights / Memory Palace Subpages

Change: Dreaming can now integrate ChatGPT imported content and directly view imported source chats, compiled wiki pages, and full source pages in the UI.

Background: Previously, Dreaming leaned more toward OpenClaw’s endogenous memory flow. External imports were often “black-box入库” for users, making it difficult to verify mapping between import sources, compiled wiki pages, and original materials.

Use Cases: For example, when users import a batch of ChatGPT history conversations, they can confirm which old conversation a particular preference was extracted from, or trace back original evidence when reviewing durable memory in Dreaming.

Considerations: Import capabilities increase memory source complexity. After upgrading, pay attention to import data volume, indexing latency, and privacy boundaries, especially avoiding indiscriminate import of private chats in shared environments.

Future Evolution: Likely to move toward multi-source imports, conflict detection, evidence chain visualization, automatic summary verification, and even converting imported chats directly into claim/evidence review flows.

Control UI/webchat: Structured Rendering of media/reply/voice Directives + [embed …] Tags

Change: WebChat now renders assistant’s media, reply, and voice directives as structured chat bubbles, adds [embed …] rich output tags, and adds configuration gating for external embed URLs.

Background: These capabilities often existed as text conventions or implicit formats in the past. Users might see semi-structured raw content that wasn’t intuitive and could expose internal protocols.

Use Cases: For example, when agents return voice replies, embed videos, rich media cards, or display structured reply directives as interactive bubbles in the browser instead of confusing text.

Considerations: When upgrading, pay attention to frontend custom rendering, embed whitelists, and CSP/external link security policies. Scripts or tests relying on raw text output may need adjustment.

Tools/video_generate: URL-only Asset Delivery, typed providerOptions, Reference Audio, etc.

Change: Video generation tool adds URL-only delivery, typed providerOptions, reference audio, asset role hints, adaptive aspect ratios, and higher image input limits.

Background: Common pain points in video generation included overly large files, inconsistent provider parameters, and weak input media role expression, preventing seamless exposure of multiple video vendor capabilities.

Use Cases: For example, having agents generate videos with reference voiceovers, or passing multiple reference images marked as cover/frame/reference, returning only URLs instead of stuffing large generated files directly into memory.

Considerations: After upgrading, check if downstream consumers accept URL-only results and if additional download logic is needed. With providerOptions becoming typed, custom plugins or scripts passing wrong fields may fail earlier.

Feishu: Document Comment Session Enhancement

Change: Improved context parsing, comment reactions, and typing feedback for document comment sessions, making document threads more like instant messaging.

Background: Document comments and IM sessions differ greatly in context structure and interaction feedback. Previously, bots in document comments often behaved like “outsiders” with incomplete context and delayed feedback.

Use Cases: Directly @OpenClaw in Feishu document reviews to explain content, reply to comment threads, or add reactions to indicate processing.

Considerations: Verify comment permissions, reaction API limits, and threading ownership. If enterprise Feishu tightens bot registration methods or agent identity policies, configuration may need synchronization.

Microsoft Teams: Reaction, Reaction Listing, Graph Pagination, Delegated OAuth

Change: Teams adds reaction sending and listing, Graph pagination handling, and delegated OAuth configuration for sending reactions, while retaining application-auth read paths.

Background: Common issues with Teams integration included insufficient write operation capabilities, incomplete pagination, and inconsistent read/write authentication modes, resulting in “can see but can’t send completely.”

Use Cases: For example, bots adding 👍 to messages in Teams groups, reading existing reactions as lightweight signals, or paginating through large channel history for context.

Considerations: Delegated OAuth typically means more complex tenant authorization and token lifecycle management. Confirm administrator consent and scope when upgrading.

Plugins: Manifest Declaration of Activation and Setup Descriptors

Change: Plugin manifests can now declare activation and setup descriptors to describe authentication, pairing, and configuration steps without hardcoding special logic in core.

Background: When plugin onboarding relies on core hardcoding, extensibility suffers, new plugin integration costs increase, and setup processes easily scatter across documentation, code, and UI.

Use Cases: A third-party provider plugin can declare “requires API Key + profile selection + device pairing,” allowing consoles or TUIs to automatically guide users through configuration based on descriptors.

Considerations: Plugin authors need to follow manifest schema changes. Old plugins without these fields should still run but need upgrades to get new setup experiences.

Detailed Analysis of Key Fixes

OpenAI/Codex OAuth: Fix authorize URL Scope Rewriting Causing invalid_scope

Change: Stop rewriting upstream authorize URL scopes to prevent new Codex logins from failing with invalid_scope before obtaining authorization codes.

Background: In OAuth flows, if scopes are incorrectly modified, users get stuck in the first half of login, experiencing “why does official login report scope error from the start?”

Use Cases: New deployments or re-logins to Codex provider no longer get blocked by incorrect scopes.

Audio transcription: Disable Pinned DNS Only for OpenAI-compatible Multipart Requests

Change: Only disable pinned DNS for OpenAI-compatible multipart transcription requests while continuing hostname validation, restoring compatibility for OpenAI, Groq, Mistral transcription.

Background: Strict network security policies conflicted with multipart upload compatibility, potentially causing some transcription requests to fail due to DNS pinning mechanisms.

Use Cases: When users upload audio to OpenAI-compatible STT backends, transcription finally works normally instead of being mistakenly blocked by network protection.

macOS/Talk Mode: No Secondary Switch Required After First Microphone Authorization

Change: After first opening Talk Mode and granting microphone permission, the flow continues automatically instead of requiring users to click again.

Background: Typical desktop permission flow issue where UI/logic doesn’t continue after authorization state changes, making users think features are broken.

Use Cases: Smoother first-time Talk Mode activation for new users, especially reducing one blocking step during demos or initial onboarding.

WhatsApp: Default Account Resolution and Reaction Path Fixes

Change: One fix ensures active listener helper correctly uses configured default account when account id isn’t explicitly passed; another fixes react actions using gateway-owned action paths, enabling active listener usage in both private and group chats.

Background: Inconsistent WhatsApp multi-account and listener ownership paths could cause subtle issues like “messages can send but reactions can’t” or “default account incorrectly registered as default.”

Use Cases: In multi-WhatsApp account deployments, default account configurations finally work as expected, and reactions become as stable as message send/poll.

ACP/agents + Codex/QA: Suppress Child Assistant Commentary Leakage and Harness Metadata Exposure

Change: ACP parent flow updates no longer expose commentary-phase child assistant relay text; Codex QA also treats app-server coordination chatter as leakage and adds live leak scenarios.

Background: In multi-agent/ACP orchestration, internal progress chatter easily mixes into user-visible output, affecting experience and potentially exposing internal implementation details.

Use Cases: Users in parent sessions only see outputs they actually need to see, no longer seeing internal chatter from child sessions or harness coordination text.

Summary and Upgrade Recommendations

Upgrade Recommendations

  1. Priority Testing Scenarios:

    • If you rely on Codex, WebChat rich media, Teams/Feishu, video generation, Ollama, local Talk Mode, this pre-release is worth testing soon
    • Production environments should use gradual rollout, focusing on OAuth login, WhatsApp reactions, multi-provider video generation, ACP visible output boundaries

  2. Maintainer Focus Areas:

    • Pay attention to QA parity gate, packaging behavior, and timeout strategy changes
    • If internal debugging relies on leaked outputs, switch to dedicated logs or verbose channels after upgrade

Future Trends

  1. Platform Evolution:

    • OpenClaw is transitioning from “strong feature stack” to “strong operations, strong visibility, strong plugin declarative capability platform”
    • Memory line will continue toward external knowledge imports, evidence chains, and Dreaming review consoles

  2. Multimodal Unification:

    • Multimodal tool layer will continue strengthening unified abstraction, but provider capability negotiation will become increasingly important
    • Visible output and internal debug output isolation will become stricter, especially in ACP, Codex, QA

  3. Enterprise Integration Deepening:

    • Integration depth for enterprise collaboration scenarios like Teams, Feishu continues to strengthen
    • Plugin ecosystem moves toward declarative, self-describing direction, reducing integration costs

Competitive Comparison Summary

  • Compared to lightweight frameworks: OpenClaw emphasizes more platformization and enterprise collaboration integration, leading in channel consistency, packaging quality, operational visibility
  • Compared to complex orchestration systems: OpenClaw’s advantage lies in integrated experience and progressive complexity control
  • Compared to minimal implementations: OpenClaw leads significantly in plugin declarations, QA governance, channel consistency, and multimodal provider abstraction, though with higher complexity

OpenClaw Active Memory Deep Guide: Making AI Remember Who You Are

Introduction: Core Pain Points of AI Memory Systems

Most AI memory systems are passive—either waiting for users to explicitly say “remember this,” or relying on the main model to decide “it’s time to search memory.” This passive model has a fundamental problem: By the time the model realizes it needs to search memory, the optimal timing has often passed.

Memory Failures in Real-World Scenarios

Consider these common situations:

  1. Dietary preferences: You mentioned hating cilantro last week, today you ask “what should I eat tonight?” and AI recommends cilantro salad
  2. Travel habits: You prefer window seats, China Eastern Airlines membership, but when asking “help me book a flight,” AI doesn’t know this information
  3. Schedule patterns: You play badminton every Saturday, but when asking “weekend plans?” AI completely forgets this routine

This information is stored in the memory system, but the main model never queries it when generating responses. This is the limitation of traditional memory systems.

What is Active Memory?

Active Memory is a core feature introduced in OpenClaw 2026.4.10, offering a direct and effective solution:

Before the main response is generated, insert a lightweight memory sub-agent to search for relevant memories, inject results into context, then let the main model generate responses based on enhanced context.

Core Design Philosophy

  1. Active rather than passive: No longer waiting for user prompts or model self-awareness
  2. Lightweight and efficient: Specially optimized memory search agent
  3. Seamless integration: User-unaware, natural experience
  4. Secure and controllable: Strict tool restrictions and timeout mechanisms

Detailed Working Principles

Technical Architecture

Key Design Features

  1. Blocking execution: Main response waits for memory search to complete, ensuring context integrity
  2. Hard timeout protection: Default 15-second timeout, automatically skips if exceeded, avoiding system hangs
  3. Tool restrictions: Sub-agent can only use memory_search and memory_get tools, preventing unexpected behavior
  4. User-unaware: Memory results injected into hidden system context, users see smarter responses
  5. Memory isolation: Each agent has independent SQLite database, ensuring privacy and security

Practical Application Scenarios

Scenario 1: Automatic Personal Preference Recall

Background: User previously mentioned “I like dark themes,” “I use Vim keybindings,” “I hate YAML format.”

Conversation:

  • User: “Help me configure the editor.”
  • Without Active Memory: AI gives generic configuration suggestions
  • With Active Memory: Sub-agent searches preferences, main model directly provides dark theme + Vim keybindings configuration, skipping YAML format

Scenario 2: Long-term Project Context Maintenance

Background: User discussed last week “We’re migrating services from Docker Compose to K8s.”

Conversation:

  • User: “How to modify the deployment script?”
  • Without Active Memory: AI doesn’t know migration background, might ask “What deployment method do you use?”
  • With Active Memory: Sub-agent searches migration context, main model directly provides K8s migration-based solutions

Scenario 3: Multi-agent Cluster Personalization

Background: System has 17 agents, responsible for development, operations, QA, product, etc.

Advantage: Active Memory enables each agent to remember user preferences and historical decisions related to its domain, rather than starting from scratch each time, achieving true personalized service.

Detailed Configuration Methods

Basic Configuration

Add to plugins.entries in openclaw.json:

Deep Analysis of Core Parameters

precision-heavyPreciseShortTechnical decisions, avoid incorrect memories

Other Key Parameters

  • timeoutMs: Memory search timeout, default 15000ms (15 seconds)
  • maxSummaryChars: Maximum memory summary characters, default 220
  • allowedChatTypes: Restrict trigger scenarios, ["direct"] means only private chats trigger
  • persistTranscripts: Whether to keep sub-agent transcripts, enable for debugging
  • logging: Whether to record debug logs, recommended during tuning

Deployment and Verification

Verifying Active Memory Works

Method 1: /verbose Debug Mode

Enable detailed mode in conversation:

Then observe Active Memory debug output to confirm if memory search triggers.

Method 2: Status Check Commands

Method 3: Gateway Log Monitoring

With logging: true enabled, view real-time logs:

Method 4: Underlying Memory System Check

Method 5: Manual Comparison Test

  1. Mention a preference in conversation (e.g., “I like using Markdown”)
  2. Start new session, enable /verbose on
  3. Ask related but not direct question (e.g., “How to write documentation?”)
  4. Observe if Active Memory recalls relevant memories

Performance Tuning Guide

Common Issues and Solutions

Issue 1: Memory recall too “noisy” (too many irrelevant memories)

Solutions:

  1. Lower maxSummaryChars value (e.g., from 220 to 150)
  2. Switch promptStyle to strict or precision-heavy
  3. Optimize memory storage, delete outdated or low-quality memories

Issue 2: Response too slow

Solutions:

  1. Lower queryMode to message (fastest)
  2. Shorten timeoutMs (e.g., from 15000ms to 10000ms)
  3. Check network and storage performance

Issue 3: No memory recall

Solutions:

  1. Confirm openclaw memory status --deep shows normal
  2. Check if agent id is in configuration list
  3. Verify if memories are successfully stored

Issue 4: Need deep debugging

Solutions:

  1. Temporarily enable persistTranscripts: true
  2. Analyze generated transcript files
  3. Disable this option after completion to avoid file accumulation

Best Practice Recommendations

1. Progressive Deployment Strategy

Phase One: Single agent testing

  • Select most used agent (e.g., main)
  • Use queryMode: "recent" and promptStyle: "balanced"
  • Observe usage for one week

Phase Two: Core agent expansion

  • Extend to core agents like development, operations
  • Adjust parameters based on use cases
  • Collect user feedback

Phase Three: Full deployment

  • Enable Active Memory for all agents
  • Establish monitoring and alerting mechanisms
  • Regularly optimize configurations

2. Memory Quality Management

Storage principles:

  • Store information with long-term value
  • Avoid storing temporary, context-sensitive content
  • Regularly clean outdated memories

Categorization suggestions:

  • Personal preferences: UI themes, editor settings, commonly used tools
  • Project context: Tech stack, architecture decisions, team agreements
  • Work habits: Meeting times, communication methods, report formats

3. Security and Privacy Considerations

Isolation strategy:

  • Independent database per agent, avoiding information leakage
  • Encrypted storage for sensitive information
  • Regular security audits

Access control:

  • Only authorized agents can access relevant memories
  • Implement memory access logging
  • Support memory deletion and correction

Technical Architecture Advantages

Comparison with Traditional Memory Systems

FeatureTraditional Memory SystemsOpenClaw Active Memory
Trigger methodPassive waitingActive searching
Response timingMay miss optimal timingAutomatically triggers before response
User experienceRequires explicit promptsCompletely unaware
System overheadIntegrated in main modelIndependent lightweight sub-agent
ControllabilityLimitedHighly configurable

Comparison with Competitive Solutions

Compared to prompt engineering-based memory:

  • Lower token consumption
  • More precise memory recall
  • Better performance

Compared to external knowledge bases:

  • Tighter integration
  • Lower latency
  • Better privacy protection

Future Evolution Directions

Short-term Improvements (2026.Q2)

  1. Intelligent memory filtering: Automatically filter irrelevant memories based on context
  2. Memory weight system: Adjust memory priority based on usage frequency
  3. Cross-agent memory sharing: Controlled information sharing mechanism

Medium-term Planning (2026.Q3-Q4)

  1. Multimodal memory: Support non-text memories like images, audio
  2. Memory relationship graph: Establish relationships between memories
  3. Predictive memory: Predict user needs based on patterns

Long-term Vision (2027+)

  1. Distributed memory network: Cross-instance memory synchronization
  2. Federated learning memory: Privacy-preserving collective memory optimization
  3. Emotional memory understanding: Understand emotions and intentions behind memories

Summary

OpenClaw Active Memory represents an important evolution direction for AI memory systems: from passive storage to active service. Through lightweight, efficient, and controllable design, it solves core pain points of traditional memory systems, providing users with truly personalized intelligent interaction experiences.

Core values:

  1. ✅ Active intelligence: AI actively remembers users, not passively waits
  2. ✅ Seamless experience: User-unaware natural interaction
  3. ✅ High controllability: Flexible configuration and tuning options
  4. ✅ Secure and reliable: Strict isolation and protection mechanisms

Action recommendations:

  1. Try immediately: Deploy Active Memory in test environment
  2. Optimize progressively: Start small, gradually tune parameters
  3. Continuous feedback: Collect user feedback, continuously improve experience

Active Memory is not just a technical feature enhancement, but a key step in AI assistants evolving from “tools” to “partners.” It enables AI to truly begin understanding and remembering each unique user, opening a new chapter in personalized intelligent services.

Introduction: Why Default Ports Are Security Risks?

In cybersecurity, default configurations are often the biggest security vulnerabilities. OpenClaw’s default port 18789 is a classic example. This port number is documented in official documentation, tutorials, and README files, making it a public target for automated scanners.

📊 Real Threat Data

  • 330,000+ OpenClaw instances exposed to public internet - According to real-time monitoring site openclaw.allegro.earth
  • Shodan search results: product:"OpenClaw" port:18789 returns thousands of exposed instances
  • Masscan scanning cost: masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p18789 --rate=10000 can scan the entire internet in hours
  • Public exploit tools: Tools like OpenClaw-PwnKit can directly obtain reverse shells

1.2 Why is Port 18789 So Dangerous?

  3. Low scanning cost: Scanning single port vs full port range
  4. High success rate: Almost everything found is an OpenClaw instance

Step 2: Solution — Changing Default Port

Before modification:

  • Faces hundreds of automated scans daily

After modification:

  • Disappears from public scanning radars
  • Scanning cost increases 65,535x (full port scan vs single port scan)
  • Attackers need targeted probing

Step 5: Advanced Security Recommendations

5.1 Combining with Other Security Measures

  1. Firewall rules: Restrict source IP access
  2. Reverse proxy: Hide real port behind Nginx/Apache proxy
  3. VPN/Tailscale: Access only within internal network or encrypted channels
  4. Authentication strengthening: Enable token authentication, IP whitelisting

5.2 Monitoring and Alerting

5.3 Regular Security Audits

  1. Monthly checks: Shodan, Censys, and other public scanning results
  2. Port scanning: Regularly scan your own public IP
  3. Configuration review: Check if security configurations were accidentally modified

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Will changing port affect OpenClaw functionality?

A: No. All OpenClaw functions are based on HTTP API, port is just the access entry point.

Q2: Do all clients need to be modified?

A: Yes, all clients connecting to OpenClaw via HTTP need port updates.

Q3: Can I use randomly generated ports?

A: Yes, but ensure client configurations are synchronized and recorded in a secure location.

Q4: What if connection issues occur after modification?

A: Troubleshooting steps:

  1. Confirm Gateway process is running normally
  2. Verify port listening status
  3. Check firewall rules
  4. Revert to original configuration for testing

Q5: Is this the only security measure needed?

A: No. Changing default port is the first step in basic security hardening, should be combined with other security measures for defense in depth.

Summary

Changing OpenClaw’s default port is a low-cost, zero-risk, high-return security hardening measure. Through this simple change, you can:

  1. ✅ Immediately reduce 90%+ automated attack risk
  2. ✅ Disappear from public scanning radars
  3. ✅ Increase attacker probing costs
  4. ✅ Lay foundation for subsequent security hardening

Security is not a one-time task, but an ongoing process. Start by changing the default port, then gradually build a complete security protection system.

This is Lesson 1 of the OpenClaw Security Hardening Series. Subsequent lessons will cover advanced topics like SSH security, authentication hardening, network isolation, etc.

💥 4 Breaking Changes

1. --custom-content Removed, Switching to Marketplace Plugin Installation

The old custom content installation relied on local filesystem paths — manually maintaining module locations and versions, error-prone in team collaboration, and unable to support community ecosystem.

v6.3.0 completely removes the --custom-content flag and all related code (custom-handler.js, custom-module-cache.js, custom-modules.js), completing the transition from “local-first” to “registry-first.”

Migration: Use --custom-source flag or the marketplace browser:

⚠️ CI/CD scripts and team docs using this flag must migrate.

2. bmad-init Skill Removed, Direct Config Loading

bmad-init was a middleware layer — every skill activation had to call it to parse configuration. It introduced Python dependency, added latency, and was error-prone.

Now all 9 agents and 12 workflow skills load directly from {project-root}/_bmad/bmm/config.yaml. Custom skill development is simpler — no need to understand bmad-init’s API, just read the file.

3. spec-wip.md Singleton Killed, Parallel Sessions Enabled

This is the core quick-dev change. The previous spec-wip.md was a global singleton — only one spec could be edited at a time. Two agents running quick-dev simultaneously would overwrite each other.

Now it’s spec-{slug}.md + status field (draft/done):

  • Multiple stories develop in parallel without interference
  • Slug collisions auto-recover existing drafts
  • Completed specs (status: done) are automatically recognized as context

This is the first true parallel session support in AI-assisted development frameworks.

4. Three Agents Merged into Developer Agent (Amelia)

Barry (quick-flow-solo-dev), Quinn (QA), and Bob (Scrum Master) are all merged into Amelia. She now has DS (design), CR (code review), and QD (quick-dev) triggers.

No more switching between 4 agents — reflecting the industry trend: from “multiple small agents” back to “one capable agent + multiple skills.”

🎁 13 New Features

Marketplace Ecosystem Trio

Universal Source Support (5-Strategy PluginResolver Cascade)

New plugin-resolver.js supports installing modules from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, self-hosted Git, and local paths. 5 resolution strategies cascade, with comma-separated multi-source support, path traversal protection, and npm lifecycle guards.

This is the first “any Git host” module installation system in AI agent frameworks.

Community Module Browser

Three-tier selection UI: official modules → community modules (category drill-down with featured and search) → custom URL. SHA-pinned installation ensures security.

VS Code marketplace-like experience, but for AI skills. The first community module browser in AI vibe coding tools.

Remote Marketplace Registry

Module list switches from bundled config to remote registry/official.yaml, with offline fallback. Modules can update independently of framework versions.

Context Awareness Trio

Epic Context Compilation

quick-dev step-01 adds sub-agent compilation: PRD, architecture doc, UX spec, and epics documents compiled into epic-{N}-context.md. Inline fallback for runtimes without sub-agent support (Copilot, Codex, Ollama).

AI finally stops developing blindly.

Story Continuity

Automatically loads completed specs from the same epic as implementation context. Story 3 development automatically understands Story 2’s API conventions and data structures.

Planning Artifact Awareness

Spec writing automatically references architecture doc tech stack choices and PRD business constraints.

Other Features

  • bmad-prfaq Skill — Amazon Working Backwards methodology, 5-phase interactive review, unique among AI dev frameworks
  • bmad-checkpoint-preview Skill — Concern-ordered guided human review (security→performance→logic→style), for author self-review
  • One-shot Spec Trace — Quick development mode now leaves artifact tracking traces
  • Checkpoint Preview UX Improvements — Clickable spec paths, third-party edit detection
  • Junie (JetBrains AI) Platform Support — BMAD now supports 9+ platforms (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Augment, Copilot, Junie, KiloCoder, Qoder, Ona)
  • KiloCoder Support Restored
  • bmad-help supports llms.txt

♻️ Refactoring + 🐛 Fixes + 🔧 Maintenance

Party-mode merged into single SKILL.md — Simplified from multi-file workflow architecture, embodying the “right-size your abstractions” principle.

5 Bug Fixes:

  • marketplace.json version display error (monorepo false positive)
  • checkpoint-preview step-05 auto-advancing without confirmation
  • Adversarial review findings fix
  • Preserve local custom module source
  • skills/ folder fallback support

Maintenance:

  • Installer rebrand (responsive logo + blue color scheme)
  • Stop copying skill prompts by default (reduce file bloat)
  • Python 3.10+ and uv documented
  • Czech and Vietnamese complete translations
  • bmad-help rewrite, checkpoint-preview explanation page

Upgrade Guide

UrgencyAction
🔴 Must--custom-content → --custom-source
🔴 Mustbmad-init references in custom skills → direct config loading
🟡 ShouldAgent references: Barry/Quinn/Bob → Amelia
🟡 Shouldspec-wip.md scripts → spec-{slug}.md pattern
🟢 OptionalTry Epic context compilation and PRFAQ skill

Competitive Comparison

DimensionBMAD v6.3.0SuperClaudeGSDgstackSpec-Kit
Module Ecosystem✅ Marketplace + Community + Universal Source❌❌❌⚠️ Limited
Parallel Dev✅ Multi-spec parallel❌ Singleton❌❌❌
Context Awareness✅ Epic compile + Story continuity⚠️ Manual❌❌⚠️ Basic
Cross-platform✅ 9+ platforms❌ Claude Code only❌❌⚠️ 2-3
Requirements✅ Brief + PRFAQ❌❌❌⚠️ Basic
Code Review✅ Concern-based❌❌❌❌

Conclusion

BMAD v6.3.0 is the most feature-complete, ecosystem-open version of any AI-assisted development framework. The Marketplace trio transforms it from “tool” to “platform,” Agent consolidation and config simplification lower the learning curve, and context compilation takes AI’s project understanding to a new level.

The cost is upgrade effort — 4 Breaking Changes mean existing users need to migrate. But it’s worth it.

item.title: Claude Code 2.1.101 Deep Dive: New Team Collaboration Tools & Enterprise Deployment Improvements
item.content:encoded:
Claude Code 2.1.101 Deep Dive Report

Release: April 2026 (extracted from CHANGELOG.md) Previous version: 2.1.98 | Analysis generated: 2026-04-11

Overview

2.1.101 is a medium-sized update containing 2 new features, 13 improvements, and 25+ fixes. Core themes:

  1. New team collaboration tools — /team-onboarding command for one-click team onboarding guide generation
  2. Zero-config enterprise infrastructure — OS CA certificate store trusted by default, TLS proxies work out of the box
  3. Lower barriers to cloud features — /ultraplan and other remote features auto-create default cloud environments
  4. Continued stability polish — Numerous fixes for --resume, permissions, plugins, and rendering issues

1. New Features in Detail

1.1 /team-onboarding — Team Onboarding Guide Generator

What changed: New /team-onboarding command that automatically generates a quick-start guide for team members based on your local Claude Code usage patterns.

Background: After adopting Claude Code, each experienced user accumulates their own best practices — custom slash commands, common MCP server configurations, permission rules, workflow habits, etc. When new members join, there’s no structured onboarding material; knowledge spreads only by word of mouth.

Use cases:

  • Tech leads generating project-specific Claude Code guides for new engineers
  • Teams standardizing Claude Code configurations to ensure consistent toolchains
  • Open source maintainers providing AI-assisted development onboarding docs for contributors

Technical details:

  • Likely analyzes local settings.json, CLAUDE.md, installed plugins, MCP configurations, etc.
  • Outputs a structured document with recommended settings, common commands, and project-specific tips

Comparison with alternatives:

  • Codex CLI: No similar feature; team onboarding is entirely manual
  • Cursor: Has shareable .cursorrules, but no auto-generated onboarding docs
  • This feature reflects Claude Code’s continued investment in team collaboration

1.2 OS CA Certificate Store Trusted by Default

What changed: The OS CA certificate store is now trusted by default, so enterprise TLS proxies work without extra configuration. Set CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE=bundled to fall back to bundled CAs only.

Background: Enterprise environments commonly use TLS MITM proxies (Zscaler, Netskope, Palo Alto, etc.) for traffic inspection. These proxies use enterprise self-signed CA certificates, and Node.js doesn’t trust the OS certificate store by default, causing frequent UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE errors in corporate networks.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise users no longer need to set the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS environment variable
  • IT admins have one fewer configuration step when deploying Claude Code
  • Works out of the box behind various enterprise security gateways

Notes:

  • If you encounter certificate compatibility issues, fall back with CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE=bundled
  • This change is transparent to non-enterprise users

Historical context: 2.1.94 fixed Bedrock SigV4 auth Bearer Token issues, and 2.1.98 fixed Bedrock 403 errors with empty string environment variables. Certificate trust is another important fix for enterprise deployment pain points.

1.3 /ultraplan Auto-Creates Default Cloud Environments

What changed: /ultraplan and other remote session features now automatically create a default cloud environment without requiring prior setup in the web UI.

Background: Previously, using /ultraplan required first visiting the claude.ai web UI to create a cloud environment — a prerequisite that often confused users: “I’m working fine in the terminal, why do I need to open a browser?”

Use cases:

  • Start using /ultraplan immediately on first use without interrupting your workflow
  • Lower the barrier to remote features, letting more users experience cloud capabilities

2. Key Improvements

2.1 Brief Mode Enhancement

Claude now automatically retries once when it responds with plain text (instead of structured messages) in brief mode. This reduces occasional formatting anomalies in brief mode.

2.2 Focus Mode Improvement

Claude now knows that users can only see the final message in focus mode, so it writes more self-contained summaries. Previously, context from intermediate steps could be lost, resulting in summaries missing key information.

2.3 Significantly Better Error Messages

This update substantially improves several categories of error messages:

  • Tool unavailable errors: Now explain why and guide users on how to handle it, instead of a bare error
  • Rate limit retries: Show which specific limit was hit and when it resets, replacing opaque countdown timers
  • Refusal errors: Include the specific explanation provided by the API

These improvements significantly affect daily experience, especially during heavy usage near rate limits.

2.4 --resume Supports Session Titles

claude -p --resume <name> now accepts session titles set via /rename or --name, no longer limited to session IDs. This is SDK and automation friendly.

2.5 Settings Fault Tolerance

Unrecognized hook event names in settings.json no longer cause the entire file to be ignored. Previously, a single typo could disable all configuration — this fix greatly improves config robustness.

2.6 OTEL Tracing Privacy Controls

Beta tracing now respects OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS, and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT flags. Sensitive span attributes are no longer sent by default and require explicit opt-in. This is important for enterprise compliance.

2.7 SDK query() Resource Cleanup

The SDK’s query() method now properly cleans up subprocesses and temporary files when consumers break or use await using. Previously, this could lead to zombie processes and /tmp directory bloat.

3. Security Fixes

3.1 LSP Command Injection Vulnerability (High Severity)

Fix: Patched a command injection vulnerability in LSP binary detection via the POSIX which fallback path.

Risk assessment: This is an exploitable security vulnerability. Attackers could potentially execute arbitrary commands through a crafted LSP server path. All users should upgrade as soon as possible.

3.2 Permission System Fixes

  • permissions.deny rules now correctly override PreToolUse hook’s permissionDecision: "ask" — previously hooks could downgrade deny to prompt
  • Fixed an issue where background cleanup ignored cleanupPeriodDays and deleted session history older than 30 days when --setting-sources didn’t include user

4. Notable Bug Fixes

4.1 --resume Fixes (4 items)

The --resume feature received extensive fixes in this release, continuing a trend across multiple recent versions:

  • Loader anchored to dead branches instead of the active conversation in large sessions, causing context loss
  • Chain resume crossed over into unrelated subagent conversations
  • Persisted Edit/Write tool results missing file_path caused crashes
  • Multiple UI issues with the /resume picker (narrow viewport, unreachable Windows Terminal preview, incorrect workspace cwd, etc.)

4.2 Timeout & Backend Compatibility

Fixed a hardcoded 5-minute request timeout that previously ignored API_TIMEOUT_MS settings and interrupted slow backends (local LLMs, extended thinking, slow gateways). This is especially important for users running local models or self-hosted deployments.

4.3 Subagent Fixes (3 items)

  • Subagents didn’t inherit dynamically injected MCP server tools
  • Subagents in isolated worktrees were denied read/write access to files within their own worktree
  • Bedrock SigV4 auth failed when an Authorization header was set

4.4 Plugin System Fixes (5 items)

  • Slash commands conflicting with plugin parsing due to duplicate name: frontmatter
  • /plugin update failing with ENAMETOOLONG
  • Discover showing already-installed plugins
  • Directory-source plugins loading from stale cache
  • Skills not respecting context: fork and agent frontmatter fields

4.5 Rendering & UI Fixes

  • Flickering on content changes in non-fullscreen mode
  • Terminal scroll buffer being cleared in long sessions
  • Mouse scroll escape sequences leaking into prompt input
  • ctrl+], ctrl+\, ctrl+^ not triggering in terminals that send raw C0 control bytes
  • /login OAuth URL rendered with extra padding

4.6 Other Important Fixes

  • Crash when environment variable values in settings.json are numbers instead of strings
  • Custom key bindings not loading on Bedrock, Vertex, and other third-party providers
  • claude --continue -p not correctly continuing sessions created by -p or SDK
  • Grep tool ENOENT when embedded ripgrep path is stale (VS Code extension auto-updates, macOS App Translocation)
  • /btw writing a full conversation copy on every use
  • Multiple Remote Control issues fixed

5. Version Jump Explanation

The version jumps from 2.1.98 directly to 2.1.101, skipping 2.1.99 and 2.1.100. This occasionally happens in Claude Code’s version history, typically because intermediate versions had issues discovered during internal testing and weren’t released publicly, or version numbers were allocated to hotfix branches.

6. Upgrade Recommendations

Must Upgrade ⚠️

  • The LSP command injection vulnerability is the most critical security fix — all users should upgrade ASAP
  • Users of the --resume feature will see significant stability improvements

Recommended Upgrade 👍

  • Enterprise users will benefit from CA certificate trust and OTEL privacy controls
  • Users with local LLMs or slow backends are no longer constrained by the 5-minute hard timeout
  • Heavy plugin users will benefit from multiple fixes

Optional Upgrade

  • /team-onboarding is valuable for team leads but not urgent
  • Brief mode and Focus mode improvements are quality-of-life enhancements

7. Trend Observations

  1. --resume is the biggest ongoing stability challenge: 5+ consecutive versions have included numerous /resume-related fixes, indicating the extreme complexity of session persistence and recovery
  2. Enterprise deployment barriers keep falling: From Bedrock wizard (2.1.92) → Vertex AI wizard (2.1.98) → CA certificate trust (2.1.101), enterprise-friendliness improves steadily
  3. Plugin ecosystem is maturing but still fragile: Every version includes plugin-related fixes, indicating the plugin system is still iterating rapidly
  4. Team features are emerging: /team-onboarding is the first explicitly team-collaboration-oriented feature, signaling Claude Code’s evolution from a personal tool to a team tool

item.title: GBrain Setup Guide: Building a Durable Knowledge Brain for AI Agents
item.content:encoded:
GBrain Setup Guide: Building a Durable Knowledge Brain for AI Agents

Your AI agent is smart, but it does not know your world by default. GBrain fills that gap.

AI agents are powerful, but they still suffer from one persistent limitation: they can talk, yet they do not truly remember your world.

Session context can carry one interaction. Memory tools can preserve preferences and decisions. But when you want an agent to retain projects, people, meetings, concepts, and long-running knowledge, you need something closer to a real knowledge brain. That is exactly where GBrain fits.

This guide covers three things:

  1. What problem GBrain actually solves
  2. Why its architecture fits agents especially well
  3. How to run a scalable local setup with PostgreSQL and pgvector

What problem does GBrain solve?

Most teams try one of four approaches first:

ApproachCommon limitation
Stuffing context into promptsExpensive in tokens, limited by context windows
Traditional RAGRe-derives answers from raw documents every time
Session memoryUseful only inside the current conversation
Agent memoryGreat for preferences and rules, not full world knowledge

GBrain has a much clearer role: it is not just a retrieval layer, it is a long-term knowledge layer for agents.

That means it is designed to support a stable loop:

That loop is what many agent systems are still missing. Without it, the model starts half-fresh every time. With it, knowledge begins to compound.

What GBrain is not

It helps to define the boundaries clearly:

  • It is not plain RAG, because it emphasizes pre-compiled knowledge rather than rebuilding everything at query time.
  • It is not just a vector database, because it also supports full-text search, explicit links, tags, and timelines.
  • It is not a normal note-taking app, because the agent itself can actively maintain the system.

A three-layer memory architecture

GBrain makes the most sense inside a three-layer model:

LayerStoresTypical access
GBrainPeople, projects, concepts, meetings, ideasgbrain search / gbrain get
Agent MemoryPreferences, operating rules, decisionsmemory_search
Session ContextThe current conversationAutomatic

These layers do not replace each other. They complement each other.

Core architecture: Compiled Truth + Timeline

One of GBrain’s smartest ideas is splitting each page into two layers.

1. Compiled Truth

The upper half is the current synthesized state.

It should stay updated and readable enough that a person or an agent can understand the situation quickly. This section is ideal for:

  • current conclusions
  • known facts
  • key relationships
  • open threads
  • cross-references

2. Timeline

The lower half is append-only history.

Instead of rewriting the past, it preserves the evolution of knowledge, such as:

  • what happened on a given date
  • where the information came from
  • when an open thread was resolved
  • when a conclusion changed

This is one reason GBrain feels stronger than classic RAG for agent workflows: the synthesis is already done ahead of time.

How the search modes differ

In practice, GBrain gives you at least four useful access patterns:

ModeCommandBest for
Keyword searchgbrain search "query"Known terms and precise lookups
Hybrid searchgbrain query "question"Semantic retrieval and broader recall
Direct readgbrain get page-slugFastest path when you know the slug
Graph traversalgbrain graph slug --depth 2Exploring relationships between entities

A nice detail is that the system is still useful even before embeddings are configured. Keyword search alone can already support a lot of real work.

Where it shines in practice

Multi-agent knowledge isolation

If you run several agents at once, it is usually better not to force them all into one shared brain. A cleaner pattern is one database per agent, selected through environment variables.

That gives you:

  • natural isolation
  • less cross-contamination between responsibilities
  • easier debugging, migration, and stats

Brain-first lookup

Before answering, the agent searches the brain instead of guessing.

That sounds obvious, but it matters a lot. A model’s internal impression gets stale quickly. The knowledge files and database are much closer to the current truth.

Automatic knowledge accumulation

A good knowledge system should not only answer, it should grow.

When an agent learns something from a meeting, conversation, email, or task flow, it should be able to turn that into structured pages and update existing knowledge instead of leaving everything trapped in chat logs.

Cross-entity reasoning

For example:

  • Who is connected to both of these projects?
  • When did this idea first appear?
  • Which later pages reference this meeting outcome?

Those queries are awkward with plain grep, but feel natural inside a knowledge system with links and graph structure.

Why choose PostgreSQL + pgvector locally

GBrain can run on lighter default engines, which is great for solo and simpler setups. But if your goals include:

  • multiple agents using it in parallel
  • long-lived databases
  • admin interfaces
  • connection pooling
  • future expansion into embeddings and richer search

then PostgreSQL + pgvector is a sturdier foundation.

A practical local service stack

A useful local stack often includes:

  • PostgreSQL + pgvector as the main database
  • Adminer for quick inspection
  • pgAdmin for heavier admin tasks
  • PgBouncer for connection pooling

The appeal is simple: stable, visible, and well suited to multi-agent use.

A safer way to initialize the system

If you want to assign separate databases to multiple agents, a few rules help a lot:

  1. use a consistent naming convention for databases
  2. keep all credentials in environment variables or a secrets manager
  3. enable required extensions like vector and pg_trgm
  4. initialize schema first, then import each workspace

The most important publishing rule is simple: never expose real passwords, email addresses, internal hostnames, or private project identifiers in public articles.

A sensible initialization flow

A typical sequence looks like this:

  1. start the PostgreSQL stack
  2. create one database per agent
  3. install the gbrain CLI
  4. run gbrain init --url ...
  5. import workspaces with gbrain import
  6. document the operating rule: search first, answer second, write back third

I strongly recommend making these four rules explicit:

  • Brain-first lookup
  • Write what you learn
  • Read before creating
  • Corrections are highest priority

Designing sync jobs safely

If you plan to sync multiple workspaces on a schedule, parallel import is fine, but do not rely on one shared global config file. A more reliable pattern is to pass each process its own GBRAIN_DATABASE_URL.

That avoids race conditions and makes each agent’s sync job clearer and more isolated.

On top of that, a practical schedule might be:

  • sync content every 30 minutes
  • check for new GBrain releases daily
  • refresh embeddings only when needed

How to verify the installation

A useful verification order is:

  1. gbrain doctor --json
  2. gbrain stats
  3. gbrain search "known-keyword"
  4. run one end-to-end sync test
  5. confirm different agents show different stats

If all of those pass, the system is already in a solid usable state.

A pragmatic rollout plan

My recommendation is to enable it in two stages.

Phase 1: get the free core working

  • store pages, indexes, and links in PostgreSQL
  • use gbrain search for keyword retrieval
  • import content with gbrain import --no-embed

This keeps costs low and lets you prove the value of the knowledge loop quickly.

Phase 2: add embeddings and hybrid search

Once the workflow is stable, then add model API keys and enable:

  • vector embeddings
  • hybrid retrieval
  • query expansion
  • more integration recipes

That gradual path is usually much easier than trying to turn on everything at once.

Why GBrain is worth serious attention

A lot of so-called AI memory systems really just pile up old content and hope the model can recover meaning later. GBrain feels more ambitious in a good way. It tries to give agents a real knowledge infrastructure.

Its value is not only that it can search. It is that:

  • knowledge can be continuously organized
  • state can be repeatedly updated
  • relationships can be made explicit
  • change over time can be preserved

That is what starts moving an agent from “able to answer” toward “actually knows what is going on.”

Closing thought

If you are pushing agents beyond toy usage and toward long-term collaboration, GBrain is well worth evaluating.

It is not the lightest option, and it is not zero-cost in complexity. But it solves a more fundamental problem: how to let an agent’s knowledge grow over time instead of restarting from scratch.

If you want to start small, I would do just three things first:

  1. stand up one database
  2. connect one agent
  3. enforce brain-first lookup

Once that loop is real, the compounding benefit becomes hard to ignore.

item.title: GBrain: Garry Tan's Opinionated Knowledge Brain for AI Agents
item.content:encoded:
What happens when a Y Combinator president decides his AI agent isn’t smart enough? He builds it a brain — from scratch.

GBrain is Garry Tan’s open-source knowledge brain system. It started as a simple markdown repo for his OpenClaw agent and grew into a full-blown personal intelligence platform: 10,000+ markdown files, 3,000+ people dossiers, 13 years of calendar data, and a “dream cycle” that enriches the brain while he sleeps.

This isn’t another note-taking app. It’s a compounding knowledge system where every conversation, meeting, and idea makes the agent permanently smarter.

The Core Idea: Compiled Truth + Timeline

Every page in GBrain follows a simple but powerful pattern:

  • Above the separator: Compiled truth — your current best understanding, rewritten when evidence changes
  • Below the separator: Timeline — append-only evidence trail that never gets edited

The compiled truth is the answer. The timeline is the proof. This separation is what makes GBrain an intelligence system rather than just a note dump.

The Compounding Loop

This is the key insight that separates GBrain from static note systems:

Every cycle through this loop adds knowledge. Look someone up once, and that lookup lives in the brain forever. A pattern emerges across three meetings — the agent captures it. Generate an original idea in conversation — it goes to your searchable intellectual archive.

An agent without this loop answers from stale context. An agent with it gets smarter every conversation.

Why Markdown? Why Not a Database from the Start?

GBrain’s knowledge model is just markdown files in a git repo. No proprietary format. No vendor lock-in. Human-readable, human-editable.

You don’t need Postgres to start. The skills and schema work with any AI agent that can read and write files. At 500 files, grep is fine.

But at 3,000 people pages, 5,800 Apple Notes, and 13 years of calendar data, grep falls apart. That’s when GBrain adds Postgres + pgvector — hybrid search that combines keyword matching for exact names with vector search for semantic meaning, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

The Dream Cycle

Perhaps the most fascinating feature: GBrain’s agent runs a dream cycle while you sleep. It:

  1. Scans every conversation from the day
  2. Enriches missing entities
  3. Fixes broken citations
  4. Consolidates memory

You wake up and the brain is smarter than when you went to sleep. OpenClaw ships this as DREAMS.md. It’s the agent equivalent of how human memory consolidates during sleep.

How Search Actually Works

GBrain’s search is a multi-stage pipeline:

  1. Multi-query expansion (Claude Haiku) — generates alternative phrasings
  2. Parallel search — vector (HNSW cosine) + keyword (tsvector)
  3. RRF Fusion — score = sum(1/(60 + rank))
  4. 4-Layer Dedup — best chunk per page, cosine similarity > 0.85, type diversity cap, per-page chunk cap
  5. Stale alerts — flags when compiled truth is older than latest timeline

Why both? Keyword search alone misses conceptual matches — “ignore conventional wisdom” won’t find “The Bus Ticket Theory of Genius.” Vector search alone misses exact phrases. RRF gets both right.

Architecture Overview

The repo is the system of record. GBrain is the retrieval layer. The agent reads and writes through both. Human always wins — you can edit any markdown file directly and gbrain sync picks up the changes.

Real-World Scale

These numbers come from Garry’s actual deployment:

ContentScale
Markdown files10,000+
People dossiers3,000+
Calendar events21,000+ (13 years)
Apple Notes5,800+ (since 2009)
Meeting transcripts280+
Original ideas300+
Media pages500+

Storage for ~7,500 pages: about 750MB in Postgres (text + embeddings + indexes). Supabase Pro at $25/month handles it comfortably.

What You Can Ask It

The power shows in cross-referencing queries:

“Who should I invite to dinner who knows both Pedro and Diana?” — Cross-references the social graph across 3,000+ people pages

“What have I said about the relationship between shame and founder performance?” — Searches YOUR thinking, not the internet

“What changed with the Series A since Tuesday?” — Diffs timeline entries across deal and company pages

“Prep me for my meeting with Jordan in 30 minutes” — Pulls dossier, shared history, recent activity, open threads

Fat Skills, Not Application Code

GBrain’s intelligence lives in markdown skill files, not code. The CLI provides tools; the skills tell the agent HOW and WHEN to use them:

SkillPurpose
ingestImport meetings, docs, articles with entity propagation
query3-layer search with synthesis and citations
maintainFind contradictions, stale truth, orphans, dead links
enrichEnrich pages from third-party APIs
briefingDaily meeting prep with participant context
migrateUniversal import from Obsidian, Notion, Logseq, etc.

Without the skillpack, your agent has tools but no playbook. With it, the agent knows when to read, when to write, how to enrich, and how to keep the brain alive autonomously.

Getting Started

The beauty of GBrain is that you can start small:

  1. Just markdown: Create a repo with the compiled truth + timeline pattern. Any AI agent that reads files can use it.
  2. Add search: When grep isn’t enough, install GBrain CLI and connect Supabase.
  3. Add skills: Load the skillpack to make your agent autonomous.
  4. Enable the dream cycle: Let the agent consolidate and enrich while you sleep.

Works with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Claude Code (via MCP), Cursor, Windsurf — or standalone from the terminal.

The Bigger Picture

GBrain represents a fundamental shift in how we think about AI assistants. Instead of asking “how do I make my AI smarter right now?” it asks “how do I make my AI smarter over time?”

The answer: give it a memory system where every interaction compounds. Not just chat history. Not just RAG over documents. A living, growing, self-maintaining knowledge graph where the agent is both reader and writer.

Vannevar Bush imagined the Memex in 1945 — a device that would store all of a person’s books, records, and communications, mechanically indexed for instant retrieval. Eighty years later, GBrain might be the closest anyone has come to actually building it.

Overview

2026.4.10 is a heavyweight release, shipped on April 11, 2026. It contains 17 new features and 20+ fixes, covering model integration, memory systems, voice, security hardening, and multi-channel fixes.

Three highlights:

  1. Native Codex Integration — OpenAI Codex as a built-in provider, independent from the OpenAI channel
  2. Active Memory Plugin — Automatic memory recall without manual user triggers

New Features

  • Evolution: OpenClaw initially supported only a single OpenAI provider → later added multi-provider architecture (OpenRouter, Anthropic, Ollama, etc.) → this version elevates Codex to a first-class independent provider.

Supports message/recent/full context modes, /verbose real-time inspection, advanced prompt/thinking overrides, and optional transcript persistence.
  • Background: Previously, users had to manually say “remember this” or “search memory” to trigger the memory system. Useful context in daily conversations was being missed, rendering the memory system largely ineffective.

Configuration example: enable the plugin with context: "recent" mode, and the agent automatically queries recent relevant memories before each reply.
  • Notes: Adds latency to each reply (extra sub-agent call); increased token consumption; recommend starting with message mode (lightest) to evaluate before upgrading to full mode. Use /verbose to observe the recall process.

  • Notes: macOS Apple Silicon (M1+) only; experimental feature — voice quality may not match cloud services; requires downloading MLX voice models.
  • Evolution: Talk Mode: cloud TTS only → this version adds local MLX option, evolving toward a hybrid architecture.

  • What changed: Fixed /btw failure after tool-use turns, cleaned up replayed tool blocks, hidden reasoning, and malformed image payloads.

  • What changed: Command output, send strategy, usage/cost, context reports, and model lists now use the selected agent/session rather than the requester.

  4. Special attention: WhatsApp users, Teams users, and Tailscale remote management scenarios all have important fixes

  2. Local inference continues to strengthen — MLX voice is the beginning, likely expanding to local model inference

item.title: OpenClaw Active Memory: Making AI Proactively Remember Who You Are
item.content:encoded:
The Problem

Most AI memory systems are passive — they either wait for the user to say “remember this,” or rely on the main model to decide “maybe I should search my memory.” The problem: by the time the model realizes it should check, the best moment has already passed.

For example:

  • You say “what should I eat tonight?” and the AI doesn’t know you mentioned hating cilantro last week — it recommends a cilantro salad
  • You ask “help me book a flight” and the AI doesn’t know you prefer window seats and are an airline loyalty member
  • You say “weekend plans” and the AI doesn’t know you play badminton every Saturday

All this information exists in memory, but the main model simply never looked it up when generating its reply.

Active Memory’s approach is straightforward: before the main reply is generated, insert a lightweight memory sub-agent that searches relevant memories, injects the results into context, then lets the main model reply.

How It Works

Key design decisions:

  1. Blocking — the main reply waits for it to complete, not async
  2. Hard timeout — 15 seconds by default; if it times out, it’s skipped without hanging
  3. Sub-agent limited to two tools — memory_search and memory_get only; it can’t go rogue
  4. Invisible to the user — injected as hidden system context; the user just sees a smarter reply
  5. Memory isolation per agent — each agent has its own SQLite database; no cross-contamination

Real-World Scenarios

Scenario 1: Personal Preferences Surface Automatically

The user previously mentioned “I like dark themes,” “I use Vim keybindings,” and “I hate YAML.”

Now the user says: “Help me configure my editor.”

Without Active Memory: AI gives generic configuration advice. With Active Memory: sub-agent finds preferences, main model directly provides dark theme + Vim keybinding config, skipping YAML format.

Scenario 2: Long-Term Project Context

Last week, the user discussed “we’re migrating services from Docker Compose to K8s.”

Today the user says: “How should I update the deployment scripts?”

Without Active Memory: AI doesn’t know the migration context, might ask “what deployment method are you using?” With Active Memory: sub-agent finds the migration context, main model gives a solution based on the K8s migration.

Scenario 3: Personalization Across Multi-Agent Clusters

We run 17 agents, each handling different domains (dev, ops, QA, product, etc.). Active Memory lets each agent remember user preferences and historical decisions relevant to its own domain, instead of starting from scratch every time.

Configuration

Add to the plugins.entries section of openclaw.json:

Core Parameters

queryMode — how much conversation the sub-agent sees:

ModeWhat It SeesLatencyBest For
messageLatest message onlyLowest (3-5s)Quick preference recall
recentLatest message + recent turnsMedium (~15s)Recommended starting point
fullFull conversation historyHighest (15s+)Deep context needed

promptStyle — how aggressively the sub-agent returns memories:

  • balanced: General default, recommended starting point
  • strict: Conservative, prefers returning nothing
  • recall-heavy: Aggressive recall, returns soft matches too
  • precision-heavy: Extremely conservative, only exact matches
  • preference-only: Focuses on preferences, habits, tastes
  • contextual: Emphasizes conversation continuity

allowedChatTypes — which chat types activate it:

  • direct: Private chats (recommended default)
  • group: Group chats
  • channel: Channels

Verification

Method 1: /verbose on

Type /verbose on in any conversation session. Subsequent replies will include an Active Memory status line:

  • ok = running normally
  • 842ms = sub-agent duration
  • recent = query mode used
  • 34 chars = summary length injected

Method 2: /active-memory status

Check the Active Memory status for the current session:

Method 3: Gateway Logs

With logging: true, you can see Active Memory run details in the gateway logs:

Method 4: Memory Health Check

Verify the underlying memory system is working:

Method 5: Manual A/B Test

  1. Store a memory (mention a preference in conversation)
  2. Start a new session, /verbose on
  3. Ask a related but indirect question
  4. Check whether the Active Memory Debug line recalled that memory

Tuning Tips

  • Too noisy: Lower maxSummaryChars, or switch to strict / precision-heavy style
  • Too slow: Downgrade queryMode to message, shorten timeoutMs
  • No recall: Verify openclaw memory status --deep is healthy, confirm agent id is in the list
  • Debugging: Temporarily enable persistTranscripts: true to keep sub-agent transcripts (watch for file accumulation)

Our Deployment

  • Instance: Local machine (OpenClaw 2026.4.10)
  • Scope: All 17 agents
  • Memory isolation: Each agent has its own SQLite database, no cross-contamination

item.title: Claude Code 2.1.98 Deep Dive: 8 New Features + 40+ Fixes Fully Analyzed
item.content:encoded:
Release date: April 2026 (extracted from CHANGELOG.md) Previous version: 2.1.97 | Analysis generated: 2026-04-10

Overview

2.1.98 is a heavyweight update containing 8 new features and 40+ fixes and improvements. Core themes:

  1. Enterprise Platform Support Enhancement — Google Vertex AI guided setup, Perforce integration
  2. Security Overhaul — Multiple Bash permission bypass vulnerabilities fixed (CVE-level)
  3. Stability Polish — Numerous edge case fixes for /resume, MCP, and permission systems
  4. Developer Experience Improvements — Monitor tool, Vim mode enhancements, OTEL tracing refinements

I. New Features In-Depth

1.1 Google Vertex AI Interactive Configuration Wizard

Change: After selecting “3rd-party platform” on the login screen, a complete GCP guided flow is now available — authentication, project/region selection, credential verification, and model binding all in one step.

Background: Previously, Vertex AI configuration required manually setting multiple environment variables (ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID, CLOUD_ML_REGION, etc.), creating a high barrier for users unfamiliar with GCP, with configuration errors difficult to diagnose.

Use Cases:

  • Enterprise users deploying Claude Code on GCP for the first time
  • New team members quickly onboarding without reading configuration docs
  • Switching between multiple projects/regions directly through the wizard

Notes:

  • Requires gcloud CLI installed locally with basic authentication completed
  • Region selection affects latency and model availability (some models only available in regions like us-east5)
  • Model pinning writes to local config; switching requires re-running the wizard

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Relies on OpenAI API key, no platform wizard, relatively simpler config
  • Gemini CLI: Native Google product, works after gcloud auth, no additional config needed
  • Claude Code’s move closes the experience gap with Gemini CLI in the GCP ecosystem

Historical Context: 2.1.94 added Bedrock Mantle support, 2.1.97 fixed Bedrock SigV4 authentication issues. The Vertex AI wizard is a continuation of the cloud platform integration strategy.

1.2 Perforce Mode (CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE)

Change: When this environment variable is set, Edit/Write/NotebookEdit will error and prompt p4 edit when encountering read-only files, rather than silently overwriting.

Background: Large gaming, chip design, and other industries widely use Perforce (P4) for version control. P4’s workflow is fundamentally different from Git — files are read-only by default and must be checked out (p4 edit) before modification. AI coding tools directly overwriting read-only files can cause lost changes and workspace state corruption.

Use Cases:

  • Game studios using Unreal Engine + P4 for large projects
  • Chip RTL code repositories (typically 100GB+ P4 depots)
  • Any hybrid Git + P4 workflow

Notes:

  • Requires setting CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE=1 in shell profile or project .env
  • Currently only blocks writes and prompts; doesn’t auto-execute p4 edit (likely a security consideration)
  • Works best with P4’s .p4config

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI / Gemini CLI: No Perforce support; P4 users must handle it themselves
  • Claude Code is the first AI coding tool with native Perforce workflow support — a differentiator in the enterprise market

Future Evolution: Subsequent versions may add automatic p4 edit capability (requiring permission confirmation) and P4 changelist integration.

1.3 Monitor Tool — Background Script Event Stream

Change: New Monitor tool for streaming events from background scripts.

Background: Claude Code already supports running scripts in the background (subagents, long builds, etc.), but previously lacked real-time monitoring capabilities — you could only wait for completion or poll logs.

Use Cases:

  • Monitoring progress of long-running test suites
  • Watching real-time output of background build/deploy scripts
  • Debugging anomalies during subagent execution

Notes:

  • Works better in combination with the 2.1.98 fix for “background subagent failures not reporting partial progress”
  • Event stream format may change across versions

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Supports --stream output but no standalone monitoring tool
  • Gemini CLI: No background task monitoring capability yet

1.4 Subprocess Sandbox Hardening (PID Namespace Isolation)

Change:

  • On Linux, setting CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB enables PID namespace isolation
  • New CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS limits per-session script invocation count

Background: As Claude Code is used in more sensitive environments (production servers, CI/CD), subprocess isolation needs grow stronger. PID namespaces prevent subprocesses from seeing or manipulating other processes on the host.

Use Cases:

  • Restricting Claude Code subprocess permissions in CI/CD pipelines
  • Security isolation in multi-tenant environments
  • Limiting script execution count per session to prevent runaway loops

Notes:

  • PID namespace is Linux-only (macOS doesn’t support this kernel feature)
  • Requires root or CAP_SYS_ADMIN to create namespaces
  • CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS upper limit needs tuning based on workload

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker containers for isolation — coarser grained but more mature
  • Gemini CLI: No explicit sandbox mechanism yet
  • Claude Code’s approach is lighter weight, suitable for environments where Docker isn’t available

1.5 Print Mode Cross-User Cache Optimization

Change: --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections flag excludes dynamic system prompt sections in print mode.

Background: Claude Code’s print mode is used for batch/automation scenarios. Dynamic parts of system prompts (usernames, timestamps, etc.) prevent prompt cache sharing across users, wasting tokens.

Use Cases:

  • Enterprise batch code review pipelines
  • Reducing API costs in multi-user shared CI services
  • Prompt cache hit rate optimization

Notes:

  • Excluded sections may contain useful context — trade-offs required
  • Only affects print mode; interactive mode unaffected

1.6 Git Worktree Status Recognition

Change: Status line JSON now includes workspace.git_worktree field.

Background: Git worktree allows multiple working directories for the same repository, commonly used for parallel development/code review. Claude Code previously couldn’t distinguish between main and linked worktrees, potentially causing path confusion.

Use Cases:

  • Parallel PR processing using worktrees
  • Correct context identification when running Claude Code in a worktree
  • Custom status line scripts adjusting behavior based on worktree status

Notes: 2.1.97 initially added this field; 2.1.98 ensures it’s correctly set in all scenarios.

1.7 OTEL Tracing — TRACEPARENT Propagation

Change: Bash subprocesses automatically inherit the W3C TRACEPARENT environment variable.

Background: With OpenTelemetry tracing enabled, subprocess spans couldn’t properly attach to Claude Code’s trace tree, breaking distributed tracing chains.

Use Cases:

  • Enterprise observability platform integration (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger)
  • Debugging cross-process performance bottlenecks
  • Auditing all subprocess call chains triggered by Claude Code

1.8 LSP clientInfo Identification

Change: Claude Code now identifies itself via the clientInfo field in LSP initialize requests.

Background: Language servers (LSP) couldn’t distinguish between requests from Claude Code and other editors, making targeted optimization or debugging difficult.

Use Cases:

  • LSP servers adjusting behavior based on client type
  • Quick source identification when debugging LSP interaction issues

II. Security Fixes (Critical)

This version fixes multiple severe permission bypass vulnerabilities — the most critical part of this update.

2.1 Bash Tool Backslash Escape Bypass (Severe)

Issue: Backslash-escaped flags could be auto-approved as “read-only” operations while actually executing arbitrary code.

Impact: Attackers (or malicious prompts) could craft commands with backslashes to bypass permission checks, executing dangerous operations in auto mode.

Fix: Normalize escape characters before permission matching.

2.2 Compound Command Bypass of Forced Permission Prompts

Issue: Pipes, &&, ;, and other compound commands could bypass auto and bypass-permissions mode security checks.

Impact: Even with strict permission rules configured, dangerous parts within compound commands could be silently executed.

2.3 Environment Variable Prefix Bypass

Issue: Commands in ENV_VAR=value dangerous_command format, if ENV_VAR wasn’t in the known safe list, wouldn’t trigger permission prompts.

Fix: Now only known safe variables like LANG, TZ, NO_COLOR are exempt from prompts.

2.4 /dev/tcp and /dev/udp Redirections

Issue: Redirections to /dev/tcp/... or /dev/udp/... were auto-allowed, enabling data exfiltration.

Fix: Such redirections now force a prompt.

2.5 Other Permission-Related Fixes

  • --dangerously-skip-permissions silently downgraded to accept-edits after writing to protected paths
  • Admin-removed managed-settings rules remained effective until restart
  • additionalDirectories changes didn’t take effect in real-time
  • Wildcard rules Bash(cmd:*) didn’t match commands with extra spaces
  • Deny rules downgraded in pipe commands containing cd
  • grep -f / rg -f reading files outside working directory without prompting
  • JS prototype property names (e.g., toString) causing settings.json to be ignored

Overall Assessment: This is a comprehensive security audit fix. Users of auto mode or bypass-permissions should upgrade immediately.

Comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Docker sandbox; different permission model; these bypasses don’t apply
  • Gemini CLI: Simpler permission system; smaller attack surface but also fewer features

III. Stability & Experience Fixes

3.1 Streaming Response & Retry

  • Streaming response timeout now falls back to non-streaming mode (instead of failing outright)
  • Exponential backoff fix for 429 retries: previously burned through all retries within 13 seconds when Retry-After was small
  • 2.1.97 initially fixed this; 2.1.98 further refines it

3.2 Comprehensive /resume Fixes

  • --resume <name> opened as non-editable
  • Filter refresh clearing search state
  • Empty list swallowing arrow keys
  • Cross-project expiration issues
  • Task status text replacing conversation summaries
  • Added project/worktree/branch name filter indicators

3.3 Terminal Compatibility

  • Uppercase letters becoming lowercase under kitty keyboard protocol (xterm, VS Code terminal)
  • macOS text replacement deleting trigger words
  • Fullscreen mode MCP tool result hover crash
  • URL copy inserting line break spaces

3.4 MCP-Related

  • OAuth authServerMetadataUrl not taking effect for token refresh after restart
  • _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] not bypassing token persistence layer

3.5 Permission System Real-Time Updates

  • permissions.additionalDirectories changes take effect immediately
  • Removing directories no longer erroneously revokes same-named directories passed via --add-dir
  • Managed-settings rule removal takes effect immediately

IV. Improvements

4.1 /agents Tab Layout

New Running tab shows active subagents; Library tab adds “Run agent” and “View instances” actions.

4.2 Vim Mode Enhancements

NORMAL mode j/k navigates history; reaching input boundary selects footer pill.

4.3 Accept Edits Mode Intelligence

File system commands with safe environment variable prefixes or process wrappers (e.g., LANG=C rm foo, timeout 5 mkdir out) auto-approved.

4.4 Hook Error Diagnostics

Hook errors in transcripts now include first line of stderr — self-diagnosable without --debug.

4.5 DISABLE_COMPACT Refinement

With DISABLE_COMPACT set, /compact prompt no longer displayed; CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS correctly respects this setting.

V. Trend Analysis

5.1 Accelerating Enterprise Focus

Vertex AI wizard, Perforce support, PID isolation, OTEL tracing — nearly all 2.1.98 new features target enterprise users. Claude Code is evolving from “developer tool” to “enterprise development platform.”

5.2 Security Maturity Leap

Fixing 10+ permission bypass issues at once indicates Anthropic conducted a systematic security audit. This is the necessary path for AI coding tools moving toward production environments. Expect subsequent versions to continue tightening the permission model.

5.3 Multi-Platform Ecosystem

From AWS Bedrock to GCP Vertex AI, Claude Code is building a multi-cloud support matrix. Compared to Codex CLI (OpenAI only) and Gemini CLI (Google only), this is a unique competitive advantage.

5.4 SubAgent System Maturation

Monitor tool, subagent error reporting, worktree cleanup fixes — multi-agent architecture continues to evolve. Claude Code is becoming an agent orchestration platform.

VI. Upgrade Recommendations

  • Auto/bypass-permissions mode users: Upgrade immediately (security fixes)
  • GCP Vertex AI users: Recommended upgrade (new wizard dramatically lowers config barrier)
  • Perforce users: Recommended upgrade (first native support)
  • General users: Suggested upgrade (terminal compatibility and stability improvements)
