OpenClaw 2026.4.9 Deep Analysis

Generated: 2026-04-09 12:30 CST

Overall take

OpenClaw 2026.4.9 is not a flashy feature release. It is a product-grade consolidation release that pushes Memory, Auth, Security, and cross-platform consistency forward in one move.

If 2026.4.8 was about getting the system running and smoothing deployment, then 2026.4.9 is about runtime trustworthiness, memory governance, plugin extensibility, and release engineering.

This release can be grouped into six major themes:

  1. Memory and Dreaming move from experimental capability to traceable, replayable, governable infrastructure
  2. Security tightens further, especially around post-interaction safety checks, untrusted input isolation, and remote text pretending to be trusted system content
  3. Provider and Auth logic continue moving out of hard-coded core paths and into plugin-declared capabilities
  4. QA evolves from “does it work” toward comparing character, tone, and model behavior in parallel
  5. Cross-platform engineering gets stronger, especially across iOS, Android, Windows, and package integrity
  6. Many small routing, reply, and streaming bugs were fixed, which is a classic sign of a system entering the real-world reliability phase

In one sentence:

The value of 2026.4.9 is not that OpenClaw can do dramatically more, but that it looks more like a long-term operable, auditable, and safely extensible agent runtime.

Memory becomes a cognition system

The most important product signal in this release is the continued evolution of Memory and Dreaming.

Grounded REM backfill, historical REM harnesses, diary commit/reset, durable fact extraction, and live short-term promotion all point in the same direction: OpenClaw is no longer treating memory as a passive archive. It is treating memory as a managed cognitive substrate.

That matters because older agent memory systems usually had a structural split:

  • new conversations entered memory pipelines,
  • old daily logs stayed as dead files,
  • upgraded extraction logic could not replay historical notes cleanly,
  • and short-term versus long-term memory slowly diverged.

This release addresses that directly. Historical daily notes can be replayed into a newer memory pipeline, producing dream-layer summaries, durable facts, and promotion candidates. That turns old notes from static archives into reprocessable cognition inputs.

At the same time, this is a risky path. Historical contamination, duplicate fact promotion, incorrect attribution, and memory noise are real dangers. The fact that OpenClaw added grounded lanes, traceability, reset paths, and extraction hardening alongside the feature is a very good sign. It suggests the authors understand that this is a high-risk write path into the agent’s long-term mind.

Control UI becomes an observability console

The companion change is just as important: these memory and dreaming capabilities are being surfaced in a UI people can inspect and operate.

That matters because memory systems are often not limited by capability, but by explainability. Users need to see:

  • what was remembered,
  • why it was remembered,
  • what is staged versus grounded versus promoted,
  • where a durable fact came from,
  • and how to reset a questionable backfill run.

A structured diary view, timeline navigation, traceable summaries, grounded scene lanes, and backfill controls move OpenClaw closer to a true runtime observability console. It becomes much easier to debug memory behavior, audit provenance, and understand how an agent’s beliefs were formed.

This likely points toward future features such as memory lineage graphs, durable fact approval flows, confidence scores, and conflict resolution between competing facts.

QA becomes personality engineering

The QA and Lab work is another clear signal.

Character-vibes evaluation reports, model selection tools, and parallel runs show that OpenClaw is no longer satisfied with “the model works.” It is starting to evaluate whether a model behaves like the intended agent.

That is a major shift. In agent products, quality is not just factual correctness anymore. It also includes:

  • whether the tone is too verbose,
  • whether the personality drifts after a prompt change,
  • whether a fallback model still feels like the same agent,
  • whether a system prompt produces the right operational style.

This is the beginning of personality engineering as a first-class QA discipline.

Provider/Auth becomes more plugin-native

providerAuthAliases is one of the most strategically important architecture changes in this release.

It lets provider manifests declare shared authentication aliases so that related provider variants can reuse env vars, auth profiles, config-backed auth, and onboarding choices without hard-coding all of that into the core.

That is exactly the right direction for a growing plugin ecosystem. Otherwise the core becomes bloated with one-off provider rules.

But it also introduces real trust-boundary concerns, including alias collisions, untrusted plugins pretending to be bundled providers, and the risk of routing operator secrets into the wrong plugin tier. The presence of collision fixes and trust filtering around onboarding confirms that OpenClaw is trying to improve extensibility without relaxing security boundaries.

Security is maturing into zero-trust runtime discipline

The most important fixes in this release are security-related.

Post-interaction blocked-destination safety checks

This is one of the most important fixes in the release because it closes a classic browser automation gap.

A browser may start from a safe URL, but after a click, script evaluation, hook-triggered action, or batched navigation, it might be redirected toward an internal or blocked destination. If safety checks happen only at the initial request, SSRF-style bypasses become possible.

Re-running blocked-destination checks after interaction-driven navigations is exactly the kind of fix a mature agent browser needs.

Blocking runtime-control env vars from untrusted workspace .env

This is another high-value hardening fix.

If an untrusted workspace .env can override runtime control variables, browser control endpoints, or skip-server behavior, then simply opening a repository can silently alter how the agent runtime behaves. That is a supply-chain style risk. Downgrading trust in workspace .env files is the correct move.

Sanitizing remote node exec summaries as untrusted system events

This closes another critical trust boundary.

In a multi-node environment, remote command output should never be treated as inherently trusted. If remote summaries can appear as if they were genuine system messages, they can become prompt-injection carriers. Sanitizing those summaries as untrusted events is essential once the platform supports remote orchestration.

Auth-choice collisions in plugin onboarding

This is ecosystem security work. If an untrusted plugin can register an onboarding auth choice that looks like an official one, it may be able to confuse setup flows or intercept credentials. Namespace and trust-tier isolation are mandatory once plugin onboarding becomes sophisticated.

Reliability fixes matter too

A large part of the release is made of smaller fixes across routing, replies, streaming, Android pairing, Slack, Matrix, npm packaging, SDK exports, Windows updates, and model/provider handling.

Individually, these may look minor. Collectively, they are the signature of a platform that is being used heavily in the real world.

These fixes suggest OpenClaw is doing the hard work of separating internal control signals from user-visible output, preserving route correctness across sessions, keeping package artifacts installable, and making multi-surface behavior feel consistent.

Strategic trajectory

This release fits four longer trends:

1. Security is moving from big-hole patching to boundary refinement

The system is no longer only fixing dramatic holes. It is now hardening window seams: post-click navigation checks, remote event sanitization, env-var trust boundaries, onboarding namespace collisions, and package audit discipline.

2. Memory is moving from storage to cognition

The strongest message in this release is this:

OpenClaw no longer treats memory as an attachment. It is building memory into the substrate of agent cognition.

3. Provider/Auth is moving from core special-casing to manifest-driven declarations

That means fewer hard-coded provider exceptions and more provider-declared capabilities, auth flows, and public contracts.

4. Control UI is becoming a true runtime observability layer

It is no longer just a management console. It is becoming a place to inspect memory traces, route behavior, model selection correctness, and operational state.

Competitive positioning

Compared with lighter runtimes, OpenClaw is clearly choosing the heavy-platform path.

  • Against NanoClaw, it trades simplicity for breadth and platform depth.
  • Against Nanobot, it looks more like a full operating platform than a hackable lightweight runtime.
  • Against IronClaw, it is absorbing more zero-trust thinking without becoming purely security-first.
  • Against PicoClaw, it is solving scale and complexity rather than minimal footprint.
  • Against ZeroClaw, it is less architecturally pure but stronger in real-world integration and product surface.

Final conclusion

OpenClaw 2026.4.9 is a release that thickens the platform foundation.

Its real value is not in any single changelog item, but in the fact that several strategic directions move forward together:

  • memory becomes more like a cognition system
  • security becomes more like a zero-trust runtime discipline
  • provider/auth becomes more like a plugin protocol
  • QA becomes more like personality engineering
  • the Control UI becomes more like an observability center

If lighter competitors win by being small, fast, and clean, then OpenClaw is betting on something harder:

not just being an agent that can run, but being an agent platform that can be operated, audited, governed, and safely extended over time.

item.title: OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 Deep Dive: Memory Backfill, Security Hardening, and Delivery Reliability
item.content:encoded:
OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 Deep Dive: Memory Backfill, Security Hardening, and Delivery Reliability

1. The short version: what this release is really doing

OpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1 is not mainly about adding flashy features. It is continuing to close five major loops:

  1. Memory/Dreaming is evolving from an experimental feature into a replayable, auditable, operable cognition pipeline
  2. Security boundaries are getting harder, especially around workspace, browser, remote node, and plugin injection
  3. Multi-channel messaging is getting more precise, reducing duplicate replies, route drift, and internal control-token leaks
  4. Plugin and provider boundaries are becoming more stable, moving toward a real platform SDK
  5. QA, Control UI, and Mobile are getting more usable operationally, not just more feature-rich

If you run multi-instance OpenClaw environments, the most important changes in this beta are:

  • dreaming backfill and grounded lanes
  • browser SSRF fixes
  • dotenv and workspace plugin security patches
  • remote node exec event trust boundaries
  • sessions routing, reply, NO_REPLY, Slack, Matrix, and other delivery-correctness fixes
  • provider-auth aliases and plugin SDK cleanup

2. Overall trajectory

Compared with recent versions, this beta makes it even clearer that OpenClaw is moving from:

  • “an agent runtime that can chat”

into:

  • an agent OS with memory, orchestration, auditability, and safety boundaries

That direction is consistent with what we already saw around 2026.4.2 and 2026.4.5.

3. Detailed analysis by theme

A. Memory / Dreaming

1) Memory/dreaming: grounded REM backfill lane

The underlying problem

Older agent memory systems usually run into the same issues:

  • historical daily notes exist on disk, but never flow back into long-term memory
  • old and new memory paths diverge into two memory stacks
  • durable-fact extraction is noisy
  • historical replay is hard to trace or roll back

What this release is solving

The biggest improvement here is this:

old daily notes can finally be replayed into Dreams and durable memory in a grounded way, without maintaining a second memory stack.

In other words, historical notes are being absorbed into the same promotion pipeline as current memory.

Typical use cases

  1. Backfilling historical memory into an old workspace
  2. Rebuilding Dreams and durable facts after migrating an instance
  3. Extracting stable operational knowledge from historical logs

Example

Imagine a manager agent whose daily notes repeatedly mention things like:

  • after a tunnel IP change, known_hosts must be updated
  • some providers time out under specific transports
  • some reply fallbacks duplicate messages on certain channels

The ideal outcome of dreaming backfill is that these repeated observations become durable facts instead of staying buried in daily notes forever.

Cautions

  • backfill is high value, but also high risk
  • it can over-promote noisy or outdated information
  • old mistakes can become durable truths
  • source attribution can become messy if you do not inspect it carefully

A practical recommendation is to backfill in smaller batches, enable tracing, and manually review durable facts.

Relation to earlier releases

  • 2026.4.2 and 2026.4.5 looked like foundation work for dreaming and promotion
  • 2026.4.9-beta.1 starts filling in historical replay, grounded lanes, commit/reset, and traceability

2) Control UI/dreaming: structured diary view and grounded Scene lane

The underlying problem

If dreaming only exists in the background with no UI:

  • operators cannot see what the system remembered
  • they cannot tell where a promotion came from
  • mistakes cannot be reset or backfilled cleanly
  • “dreaming” turns into a black box

What this release adds

The Control UI now includes:

  • a structured diary view
  • timeline navigation
  • backfill/reset controls
  • traceable dreaming summaries
  • a grounded Scene lane
  • promotion hints
  • safe clear-grounded operations

That matters because memory is no longer just files and logs. It is becoming a visual cognition-operations interface.

Use cases

  • auditing dreaming results
  • tracing a durable fact back to a specific day
  • resetting incorrect promotions
  • cleaning grounded signals in staged backfill passes

Caution

promotion hints are still hints, not truth. The existence of safe clear-grounded also tells you the system expects staged signals to become dirty sometimes.

3) Memory/dreaming hardening and heartbeat token support

The underlying problem

Backfill is most fragile when:

  • the path is wrong
  • symlinks contaminate the read path
  • source-day tags get lost
  • diary titles are inconsistent
  • claim splitting is too aggressive
  • runtime wrappers swallow heartbeat tokens and dreaming never triggers

Why this matters

This is a sign that the project is moving from “can the feature work” to “is the input trustworthy, is metadata stable, and can we trace the result.”

B. QA / Lab / Live behavior

4) QA/lab: character-vibes evaluation reports

The underlying problem

Traditional QA usually focuses on:

  • whether a feature works
  • whether tool calls succeed
  • whether output errors out

But agent products also need to test something much harder:

  • whether style stays consistent
  • whether persona drifts
  • how different models feel under the same agent
  • which candidate model actually matches the intended character

What this release changes

It adds:

  • character-vibes evaluation reports
  • model selection
  • parallel runs

That means QA is expanding from functional correctness into behavioral and stylistic consistency.

Use cases

  • comparing multiple models under the same persona
  • checking whether an upgrade makes the agent too verbose, too cold, or too reckless
  • doing A/B model selection

Caution

vibes evaluation does not replace functional QA. Parallel runs are good for evaluation, not for live tasks with external side effects.

5) QA/live auth: fail fast on auth/runtime failures

The underlying problem

The most annoying part of live QA is not failure itself, but ambiguous failure:

  • an auth problem looks like a timeout
  • missing credentials just hang
  • runtime failures get swallowed

Why this matters

This improves error quality. Auth and runtime failures become actionable failures instead of vague timeouts.

C. Plugins / SDK / Provider auth

6) Plugins/provider-auth: providerAuthAliases

The underlying problem

Once your provider ecosystem gets bigger, you usually end up with:

  • one provider having multiple variants
  • variants that should share env vars or auth profiles
  • growing maintenance cost because the core has to special-case everything

What this release does

It lets a provider manifest declare providerAuthAliases, so variants can share:

  • environment variables
  • auth profiles
  • config-backed auth
  • onboarding choices

without adding more hardcoded logic to the core.

Caution

Shared auth is convenient, but trust and capability boundaries still matter. Shared credentials do not mean identical behavior.

7) Plugins/onboarding auth choices collision fix

The underlying problem

If an untrusted plugin can impersonate a bundled provider’s auth-choice ID, it might:

  • hijack onboarding flows
  • get closer to operator secrets
  • interfere with non-interactive install behavior

Why this matters

This is an important supply-chain and plugin trust-boundary fix.

8) Plugin SDK export cleanup, contracts, and command-status split

The underlying problem

Early SDKs often suffer from:

  • incomplete public APIs, forcing developers into private imports
  • test helpers leaking into production barrels
  • auth-only plugins pulling in too much status/context machinery

What this release is doing

  • exporting a real channel plugin base
  • exporting the web-search config contract
  • isolating test-only helpers from production code
  • adding a lightweight openclaw/plugin-sdk/command-status subpath

D. Security

9) Browser/security: interaction-driven navigation re-check

The underlying problem

SSRF defenses often catch direct access to blocked URLs, but miss the more subtle flow:

  1. open a safe page
  2. navigate through click/evaluate/hook/batched actions to a dangerous destination
  3. never re-run the safety checks after the navigation

What this release fixes

It re-runs blocked-destination safety checks for interaction-driven main-frame navigation.

Caution

Some previously working browser automations may now be blocked. That is the correct kind of breaking change.

10) Security/dotenv: block runtime-control env vars from untrusted workspace .env

The underlying problem

If a workspace .env can change runtime behavior, it opens a dangerous local injection surface:

  • browser-control overrides
  • skip-server switches
  • runtime-control env vars
  • URL-style override specifiers

Why this matters

This is a key local supply-chain defense. It makes the trust boundary explicit:

workspace config is not operator config, and an untrusted repo must not control the runtime control plane

11) Gateway/node exec events: mark as untrusted and sanitize

The underlying problem

If exec event summaries coming from remote nodes are treated as trusted system events, they can become a prompt-injection path via:

  • fake System: content
  • malicious summaries
  • contamination of later turns

What this release changes

Those remote exec summaries are now treated as untrusted system events and sanitized consistently.

12) Security/dependency audit: basic-ftp and Hono bumps

Why this matters

  • basic-ftp 5.2.1 closes a CRLF command-injection issue
  • Hono and @hono/node-server upgrades improve web-runtime security and compatibility

E. Gateway / Sessions / Chat delivery correctness

13) Reply/doctor improvements

The underlying problem

Asynchronous reply paths often fail in messy ways:

  • they use stale runtime snapshots
  • SecretRef resolution happens in the wrong context
  • expired OAuth looks like a generic failure
  • doctor output does not tell you how to re-authenticate

Why this matters

Queued replies get aligned more closely with the current runtime, and re-auth instructions become much more actionable.

14) Control UI: stale session-history reload guard

The underlying problem

Fast session switching often creates async race conditions where:

  • the left panel selects session A
  • the right panel renders transcript B

15) Gateway/chat: suppress ANNOUNCE_SKIP / REPLY_SKIP leaks

The underlying problem

Internal control tokens should never leak into the user-visible UI.

16) Auto-reply/NO_REPLY: strip glued leading NO_REPLY tokens

The underlying problem

If a silent sentinel token gets glued to a normal reply, it leaks into the user interface.

17) Sessions/routing: preserve established external routes

The underlying problem

If sessions_send follow-ups steal existing external routes, replies can end up in the wrong channel.

18) Gateway/sessions: clear auto-fallback-pinned model overrides on /reset and /new

The underlying problem

The system needs to distinguish between:

  1. explicit user model overrides
  2. automatically pinned fallback models

Otherwise stale model state survives resets unexpectedly.

19) Slack/media, Slack/ACP, and Slack partial streaming

Shared background

Channel delivery is not just about “message sent.” It also needs to handle previews, fallbacks, redirects, block rendering, and deduplication of partially streamed messages.

20) Matrix/gateway and Matrix/doctor

The underlying problem

  • sync may not be ready even though startup looks successful
  • background handler crashes can destabilize the whole gateway
  • schema changes can leave doctor unable to migrate old config cleanly

21) QQBot/media-tags

The underlying problem

Upstream message formats are often messy:

  • HTML entity angle brackets
  • slashes in URL-like attrs
  • self-closing tags

F. Mobile

22) Android/pairing and Android/manual connect

The underlying problem

Mobile pairing becomes painful when a single stale setup state poisons every later attempt.

This set of fixes focuses on:

  • cleaning stale setup-code auth
  • using fresh pairing bootstrap
  • preferring stored device tokens after bootstrap
  • pausing auto-retry in background
  • defaulting TLS manual endpoints to port 443 when the port is omitted

23) iOS: explicit CalVer pinning

The underlying problem

TestFlight and release trains often suffer from:

  • short version vs build number confusion
  • iOS release cadence drifting from gateway release cadence
  • short-version churn during rapid testing

G. Providers / Auth / Agents

24) Providers/OpenAI: default reasoning set to high

The underlying problem

If the default reasoning effort differs across transports, users get inconsistent behavior under what feels like the same configuration.

Caution

  • cost and latency may increase
  • answer quality and stability may improve

25) Providers/Ollama: native API path supports thinking output

The underlying problem

Local-model users increasingly care about visible thinking traces, but native api: "ollama" paths often lag behind in support.

26) Auth/profiles: persist explicit upserts locally

The underlying problem

When auth-profile changes depend on external CLI sync to become durable, local state can stay stale or get overwritten.

27) Agents/timeouts

The underlying problem

If timeout behavior is not unified, users see:

  • defaults that do not propagate to idle watchdogs
  • cron runs dying unexpectedly from idle limits
  • inconsistent error fields

28) Agents/failover: Z.ai code classification

The underlying problem

If vendor-specific error codes are classified incorrectly, failover behavior becomes unreliable.

29) Codex CLI: pass system prompt via model_instructions_file

The underlying problem

If Codex CLI sessions and Claude CLI sessions do not receive equivalent system prompts, their behavior can diverge in confusing ways.

H. Packaging / Build / Windows

30) npm packaging hardening

The underlying problem

Many dependency issues only appear in packed installs that no longer rely on repository node_modules layouts.

31) Windows/update: add heap headroom

The underlying problem

Windows dev updates and pnpm build preflight paths often fail because the default Node heap is too small.

4. Comparison with similar open-source products

DimensionOpenClaw 2026.4.9-beta.1NanoClawNanobotIronClawPicoClawZeroClaw
Memorydreaming, backfill, promotion, grounded tracelog-orientedoften vector recallenterprise knowledge flowlight local memoryminimal memory
Security boundaryworkspace, browser, node, plugin hardeningbasicimplementation-dependentusually strong audit focusbasicminimal
Channel reliabilitySlack, Matrix, QQ, routing, dedupe detailsusually shallowmediumstronger in enterprise IMweakvery weak
Plugin platformmanifest contracts, SDK exports, auth aliaseslimited pluginsextensible but variedenterprise-heavylightweightminimal
QA sophisticationcharacter-vibes plus live-auth QAmostly regressionmediumusually heavy enterprise QAlightlight
Control UImemory ops and session consistencysimplifiedmediumstrong admin consolesweakvery weak
Agent OS tendencyvery clearweakmediumstrong but enterprise-orientedweakextremely minimal

5. Upgrade notes and validation priorities

Production cautions

  1. do not enable dreaming backfill at full scale immediately
  2. .env security tightening may break older workflows
  3. stronger browser SSRF protections may block old automations
  4. default-high reasoning should trigger a cost review
  5. routing, fallback, and NO_REPLY behavior will feel stricter

Recommended validation order for cluster managers

  1. Security
    • workspace .env
    • browser navigation SSRF checks
    • remote node exec event sanitization
  2. Session and channel correctness
    • sessions_send route preservation
    • Slack fallback and partial streaming
    • Matrix startup and restart behavior
    • NO_REPLY / ANNOUNCE_SKIP leakage
  3. Memory and dreaming
    • historical backfill
    • grounded diary traceability
    • heartbeat token integration
  4. Providers and plugins
    • providerAuthAliases
    • local auth-profile persistence
    • plugin SDK exports
  5. Mobile and packaging
    • Android pairing
    • iOS version pinning
    • packed-install smoke tests

6. Where this is heading next

  1. dreaming will keep evolving into a formal knowledge-operations system
  2. security work will continue shifting from external attack surfaces to local and internal trust boundaries
  3. channels will increasingly look like a message-dispatch operating system
  4. the plugin platform will become more manifest-first and keep thinning the core
  5. QA will become more behavior-centric
  6. OpenClaw will look more and more like an agent OS rather than a bot framework

7. Final judgment

2026.4.9-beta.1 is a beta focused on platform maturation, safety boundaries, and cognition infrastructure.

In one sentence:

It is not aggressively adding surface-level features. It is continuing to push OpenClaw toward production-grade foundations across memory, safety, plugin architecture, channel delivery, and operational visibility.

item.title: OpenClaw Cross-Agent Cron Workflow in Practice: 1 Cron Job Chaining 3 Agents for Monitor → Research → Publish
item.content:encoded:
Date: 2026-04-09 Author: VibeSparking (compiled by vibesparking agent) Participating Agents: vibesparking (coordination), vs-claude (detection + report), vs-sites-astro (publishing)

1. Goal

Set up an hourly automated task to monitor version updates in Claude Code CHANGELOG.md. When a new version is detected:

  1. vs-claude agent generates an in-depth research report (problem background, use cases, competitive comparison, trend analysis)
  2. vs-sites-astro agent invokes the wechat-official-account-article skill to convert the report into an Astro Blog post, generate a cover image, and publish a WeChat Official Account draft

One cron job, spanning two agent sessions, fully automating the entire pipeline from detection to publication.

2. Final Architecture

3. State Management: Resumable Pipeline

The core design uses a JSON state file to enable pipeline checkpointing and resumption:

On each cron trigger, Step 0 reads the state:

  • publish == pending + report == done → jump to Step 5 (publish only)
  • report == pending + check == done → jump to Step 3 (generate report only)
  • Otherwise, start from scratch checking for new versions

This way, even if a run times out or a subagent fails, the next execution resumes from the last checkpoint.

4. The 7 Pitfalls We Hit (Lessons Learned the Hard Way)

The entire debugging process went through 7 iterations, roughly 1.5 hours.

Pitfall 1: Agent Routing Error

Initially the cron job ran on vibesparking (the default agent), and the publishing subagent was also routed to vibesparking. But the wechat-official-account-article skill lives on vs-sites-astro — vibesparking couldn’t find it.

Fix: Set the cron’s agentId to vs-claude, and specify agentId: vs-sites-astro for the subagent.

Pitfall 2: Non-Default Agents Don’t Support Persistent Sessions

We tried setting sessionTarget: "main" on the cron for a persistent session, but the platform threw an error:

cron: sessionTarget "main" is only valid for the default agent

Workaround: Switch to sessionTarget: "isolated" and compensate for missing context by reading historical report files.

Pitfall 3: Insufficient Permissions for Cross-Agent sessions_spawn

vs-claude tried sessions_spawn(agentId: "vs-sites-astro") and was denied:

agentId is not allowed for create_task (allowed: none)

After digging into the source code, we found it wasn’t tools.agentToAgent (that config key doesn’t exist) — it’s subagents.allowAgents:

Fix: Add the following to vs-claude’s config in openclaw.json:

Pitfall 4: Subagent Toolset Trimmed — Glob Not Found

The vs-sites-astro subagent called the Glob tool and got Tool Glob not found, looping through this error 60+ times in a single session.

The cause: maxSpawnDepth defaults to 1, and a depth=1 subagent has the leaf role, which lacks Claude Code built-in tools (Glob, Read, Write, etc.).

Fix: Set agents.defaults.subagents.maxSpawnDepth: 2 so depth=1 subagents become orchestrator (with full toolset).

But even after fixing the depth issue, Glob/Read/Write were still unavailable — these are Claude Code CLI built-in tools, not part of the OpenClaw agentTurn runtime.

Final solution: Explicitly state in the subagent’s task prompt:

❗❗ Do NOT use Glob/Read/Write tools! Use exec find/ls to find files, exec cat to read files, and exec tee to write files.

Pitfall 5: File Sandbox Isolation

vs-sites-astro’s Read tool couldn’t access report files under the vibesparking workspace:

Path escapes sandbox root (~/vs-sites-astro/.openclaw/workspace): /Volumes/.../vibesparking/.../report.md

Fix: In Step 5a, use exec cp to copy the report to the vs-sites-astro Astro blog directory first, so the subagent can access it within its own sandbox.

Pitfall 6: Stale Sessions Blocking New Tasks

After deleting an old cron job, its leftover session state remained running, blocking new cron executions. Tasks showed enqueued: true but never dispatched.

Fix: Manually clean up stale session states in sessions.json and restart the gateway.

Pitfall 7: Skill Path Resolution Strategy

The subagent searched for the skill using find ~/.agents/skills, but wechat-official-account-article was in vs-sites-astro’s workspace skills directory, not the global skills directory.

Fix: Define a prioritized search strategy:

  1. First check vs-sites-astro workspace skills: ~/WorkSpaces/.../vs-sites-astro/.openclaw/workspace/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
  2. Then check global skills: ~/.openclaw/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
  3. If neither found → exit with error

5. The Successful Run

StageAgentAction
Step 0vs-claudeRead state, detected publish: pending → jump to Step 5
Step 5avs-claudeexec cp report to Astro blog directory
Step 5bvs-claudesessions_spawn(agentId: vs-sites-astro) dispatches publishing subagent
Phase 0vs-sites-astroRead SKILL.md, pre-check
Phase 1vs-sites-astroRestructure article + frontmatter
Phase 1.5vs-sites-astroDispatch English translation subtask
Phase 2vs-sites-astroReuse existing cover image
Phase 3vs-sites-astroPublish WeChat Official Account draft
Phase 4vs-sites-astroCreate Issue #119 for tracking
Donevs-claudeReceived subagent callback, output final summary

Final output:

  • ✅ Research report: claude-code-2.1.98-changelog-analysis.md
  • ✅ Blog post: 2026-04-09-claude-code-2.1.98-changelog.md (with frontmatter)
  • ✅ WeChat draft: “Claude Code 2.1.98 Deep Dive: Enterprise Security Overhaul and Native Perforce Support”
  • ✅ English translation + GitHub Issue #119

6. Key OpenClaw Configuration

Required openclaw.json Settings

Critical Cron Job Parameters

Key Constraints for Subagent Task Prompts

  1. Must specify agentId: "vs-sites-astro" — otherwise the subagent runs under the caller’s agent and won’t find the target skill
  2. Disable Glob/Read/Write — unavailable in subagents; use exec (Bash) as a replacement
  3. Skill search priority — check agent workspace skills first, then global skills
  4. Copy files before accessing — cross-workspace files are sandbox-isolated; cp them first

7. Lessons Learned

LessonSolution
Non-default agent crons don’t support persistent sessionsUse isolated session + state file for checkpoint resumption
Cross-agent spawning requires explicit permissionsConfigure subagents.allowAgents
Subagent toolsets differ from main sessionsExplicitly specify using exec instead of built-in tools in the prompt
Cross-workspace files are sandbox-isolatedCopy to target workspace before accessing
Stale sessions from deleted crons block new tasksClean up sessions.json + restart gateway
Config changes may be overwritten by concurrent writesUse fcntl.flock file locking
Skill paths differ across agentsSearch by priority: workspace → global

Key takeaway: OpenClaw’s multi-agent collaboration capabilities are powerful, but cross-agent permissions, toolsets, and file sandboxes all require explicit configuration. This isn’t a limitation — it’s a security design. Each agent has its own boundaries. Understanding these boundaries is the key to designing reliable cross-agent workflows.

item.title: Upgrading OpenClaw to 2026.4.9: Gateway Entrypoint Change, Skills Path Security & doctor Auto-Fix
item.content:encoded:
Background

This post documents the complete process of upgrading OpenClaw from 2026.4.8 to 2026.4.9 on macOS (Apple Silicon) via openclaw update, along with all issues discovered and auto-fixed by openclaw doctor --fix.

If you’re running OpenClaw via Homebrew, this walkthrough can help you anticipate potential gotchas before upgrading.

The Upgrade

The upgrade command is straightforward:

Verify the new version:

The upgrade itself was smooth — the real action happened in doctor --fix.

5 Issues Found by doctor —fix

1. Gateway Entrypoint Changed

Symptom: Gateway fails to start

Cause: 2026.4.9 renamed the Gateway entrypoint from dist/entry.js to dist/index.js, but the LaunchAgent plist still pointed to the old path.

Fix: doctor --fix automatically updated the LaunchAgent plist to reference the new entrypoint.

💡 If your Gateway won’t start after upgrading, check the entrypoint path in your plist first.

2. Missing Bundled Plugin Dependencies

Symptom: 30 bundled plugins had uninstalled runtime dependencies

Affected plugins: acpx, discord, whatsapp, feishu, msteams, otel, and more

Fix: doctor --fix automatically installed all missing dependencies. This is routine after upgrades — new versions may introduce new plugin dependencies.

3. Orphan Session Transcript Cleanup

Symptom: 15 orphaned .jsonl files under ~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions/

Fix: doctor --fix archived them as .deleted.<timestamp> backups — no data was permanently deleted, keeping recovery possible.

4. Skills Path Security Check (⚠️ New Feature)

This is the most notable change in 2026.4.9.

New behavior: A new resolveContainedSkillPath() security check runs realpath() on each skill directory. If the resolved path falls outside the skills root directory, the skill is skipped.

Real-world impact:

  • 138 symlinks under ~/.agents/skills/ pointing to a plugin cache directory
  • All symlinks were blocked by the security check — only 60 real directories loaded normally
  • The symlinks were created automatically by plugin installation commands

Workaround:

⚠️ This security check prevents skills from escaping their intended directory scope via symlinks — a meaningful hardening measure. However, if you rely heavily on symlinks to manage skills, you’ll need to adjust after upgrading.

5. Pre-existing Warnings

These warnings were already present and don’t affect core functionality:

  • WeChat channel: Missing accounts.default configuration
  • Telegram channel: In first-time setup mode, DM requires pairing
  • Feishu channel: Multiple accounts with groupPolicy=allowlist but empty groupAllowFrom
  • Memory search: No embedding provider configured

Restart Timing Issue

After doctor --fix completes, it automatically triggers a Gateway restart. However, the subsequent health check may report Gateway not running.

Cause: A timing issue — the new process is still initializing (loading plugin dependencies, scanning skills directories), and the health check runs before startup completes.

Solution:

Upgrade Checklist

Based on this experience, here’s a checklist for future upgrades:

  1. ✅ Run openclaw update
  2. ✅ Verify version with openclaw --version
  3. ✅ Run openclaw doctor --fix
  4. ✅ Review doctor output — pay attention to new warnings
  5. ✅ If Gateway doesn’t auto-recover, run openclaw gateway restart
  6. ✅ Verify skills loading (especially if using symlinks)
  7. ✅ Test core functionality

Summary

The 2026.4.9 upgrade was smooth overall, with doctor --fix handling most issues automatically. The standout change is the skills path security check — if your skills directory contains symlinks, verify they’re loading correctly after the upgrade.

The security hardening direction is sound, but users who manage skills via symlinks will need a one-time migration. Back up your skills directory before upgrading, then adjust as needed.

item.title: Chat-Driven Website Deployment: A Complete Walkthrough with AI Agent
item.content:encoded:
Overview

This article documents the process of deploying a complete website with zero manual terminal operations, entirely through an AI Agent chat interface:

  1. GitHub Organization creation and repository initialization
  2. Local project cleanup, commit, and push
  3. CI/CD automated deployment pipeline setup
  4. DNS configuration (Cloudflare API)
  5. GitHub Pages custom domain attempt (failed)
  6. Cloudflare Pages deployment (succeeded)
  7. Custom domain binding
  8. GitHub Actions Secrets auto-configuration

All operations were performed by the Agent using shell commands, API calls, gh CLI, and npx wrangler. The user only needed to issue instructions and provide necessary tokens in the chat window.

1. Project Background

Goal

Set up a public website for a project group, bind a custom domain, build with Astro framework, and auto-deploy on push.

Project Structure

RepositoryTypePurpose
project-mgrPrivateCluster management main project
project-opsPrivateOperations scripts and configs
project-astroPrivateAstro website source (CI/CD entry point)
project-websitePublicBuild artifacts repo and deployment target

2. Phase One: GitHub Organization and Repository Initialization

2.1 Creating the GitHub Organization

The Agent created the organization via gh CLI with the designated GitHub account identity.

2.2 Creating Repositories

The Agent created 4 repositories via the GitHub API (3 private + 1 public).

2.3 SSH Identity Issue

During push, the default SSH identity was mapped to the wrong account, causing permission errors.

Solution: The Agent configured each repository .git/config with a dedicated SSH key and user identity.

3. Phase Two: Project Cleanup and First Push

3.1 Main Project Cleanup

The initial state was messy with many local process files. The Agent created .gitignore to exclude debug artifacts and system files, then completed the first commit and push.

3.2 Astro Project Initialization

The Agent completed:

  1. Generated .gitignore (standard Astro ignores)
  2. First commit and push
  3. Added website source files
  4. Created GitHub Actions workflow

3.3 Push Results

All 4 repositories successfully pushed to the GitHub Organization.

4. Phase Three: CI/CD Automated Deployment Pipeline

4.1 Initial Workflow

Single-job flow: checkout, build, rsync to artifact repo, push.

4.2 Dual-Channel Deployment

Restructured into three parallel stages: build, deploy-github, and deploy-cloudflare.

Key design decisions:

  • build job builds Astro and uploads artifact
  • deploy-github and deploy-cloudflare consume the artifact in parallel
  • Cloudflare deployment uses the official wrangler action

4.3 GitHub Actions Secrets Configuration

The Agent auto-configured 3 Secrets via gh CLI for repo push tokens, Cloudflare API tokens, and account identifiers.

5. Phase Four: DNS and Domain Configuration

5.1 Cloudflare DNS Configuration

The Agent completed all DNS operations via the Cloudflare API, creating CNAME records and TXT verification records.

5.2 GitHub Pages Custom Domain (Failed)

This was the biggest blocker in the entire process, consuming about 3 days.

Symptoms

  • GitHub org domains page showed the domain as verified
  • But Pages settings kept reporting: You must verify your domain before being able to use it
  • GitHub Pages API consistently returned cname: null

Troubleshooting

  1. Insufficient PAT permissions - The old PAT lacked Pages management permissions. Resolved by regenerating.
  2. DNS challenge expired - GitHub issued a new TXT challenge. The Agent updated the TXT record via Cloudflare API.
  3. Automated retry monitoring - The Agent created a cron job to retry binding every 5 minutes. All attempts failed.

Conclusion

GitHub Pages has a bug in syncing org-level domain verification to repo-level Pages attachment. DNS, tokens, and repo content were all correct - pure backend state desynchronization.

5.3 Cloudflare Pages Deployment (Succeeded)

As a parallel approach, the Agent completed:

  1. Created Cloudflare Pages project via API call
  2. First deployment - cloned the artifact repo, deployed directly with wrangler
  3. Bound custom domain via API association
  4. Updated DNS CNAME - switched from GitHub Pages to Cloudflare Pages
  5. Verified - confirmed HTTP 200, certificate auto-issued

6. Deployment Architecture

The final architecture uses a fan-out pattern: source repo pushes trigger GitHub Actions, which builds once and deploys to both GitHub Pages (as fallback) and Cloudflare Pages (production) in parallel.

7. The AI Agent Role Throughout

Operations Completed Directly by Agent

CategoryDetailsTool
Git operations.gitignore creation, commit, pushexec (git)
GitHub APIRepo creation, Pages status queries, Pages cname setupexec (curl)
Cloudflare APIDNS record creation/updates, Pages project creation, domain bindingexec (curl)
CI/CDWorkflow YAML authoring and updateswrite (file creation)
SecretsGitHub Actions Secrets configurationexec (gh CLI)
DeploymentCloudflare Pages first deploymentexec (npx wrangler)
MonitoringAutomated retry cron job creation and managementcron
DocumentationPhase reports, process documentationwrite

Operations Requiring Human Intervention

OperationReason
Provide Cloudflare API TokenSecurity credentials controlled by user
Provide GitHub PATSecurity credentials controlled by user
Trigger new domain verification challenge on GitHub webRequires browser interaction
Add Pages Edit permission to Cloudflare tokenRequires Cloudflare dashboard login

8. Lessons Learned

1. SSH Identity Conflicts

Problem: Multiple GitHub accounts sharing one machine, default SSH resolving to the wrong identity. Solution: Specify sshCommand in .git/config to use a dedicated SSH key.

2. Insufficient GitHub PAT Permissions

Problem: Fine-grained PAT missing Pages management permissions, API returning 403. Solution: Regenerate PAT with Administration + Pages Read and Write permissions.

3. GitHub Pages Domain Verification State Machine Stuck

Problem: Org domains page shows verified, but Pages backend refuses to acknowledge it. Solution: Abandon GitHub Pages custom domain, switch to Cloudflare Pages. Lesson: GitHub Pages sync between org-level domain verification and repo-level Pages attachment is unreliable. Do not fight it.

4. Cloudflare Token Permission Tiers

Problem: DNS-scoped token lacked account-level Cloudflare Pages permissions. Solution: Edit token in Cloudflare dashboard, add Account / Cloudflare Pages / Edit.

5. Cloudflare Pages Custom Domain DNS Verification

Problem: Initial CNAME set to proxied mode prevented Cloudflare Pages from seeing the CNAME. Solution: Switch to DNS only (proxied: false).

9. Timeline

TimeEvent
Day 1 afternoonCreated GitHub org + 4 repos
Day 1 afternoonFixed SSH identity issue
Day 1 afternoonMain project cleanup + first push
Day 1 afternoonAstro project init + workflow creation
Day 1 afternoonCI/CD first successful run
Day 1 afternoonCloudflare DNS configuration
Day 1 afternoonGitHub Pages custom domain binding failed
Day 1 eveningRepeated GitHub Pages retries, all failed
Day 3 afternoonDiscovered old PAT permission issue, switched to new PAT
Day 3 afternoonUpdated TXT challenge, DNS propagation confirmed
Day 3 afternoonCreated automated retry cron job
Day 3 afternoon30+ minutes of retries, GitHub Pages still refused
Day 3 afternoonDecided on parallel approach: Cloudflare Pages
Day 3 afternoonRestructured workflow for dual-channel deployment
Day 4 morningAdded Pages Edit permission to Cloudflare token
Day 4 09:05Created Cloudflare Pages project
Day 4 09:06First deployment to Cloudflare Pages
Day 4 09:06Bound custom domain
Day 4 09:07DNS CNAME switched to Cloudflare Pages
Day 4 09:08Website returns 200
Day 4 09:11GitHub Actions Secrets configuration complete

10. Final Status

  • Custom domain accessible
  • Cloudflare Pages auto-deployment ready
  • GitHub artifact repo syncing
  • CI/CD dual-channel workflow in place
  • All Secrets configured
  • GitHub Pages custom domain still unbound (no production impact)

Conclusion

This process demonstrates the capability boundaries of an AI Agent as a DevOps collaborator:

  • Excels at: API calls, CLI operations, file editing, automated retries, multi-step orchestration
  • Needs humans for: Security credential management, browser interactions, permission change approvals
  • Net efficiency: Over a 4-day span, actual human hands-on time was under 20 minutes (all token provision and operation confirmations), with everything else handled by the Agent

This is not about an Agent replacing DevOps engineers. It is about delegating the instruction execution layer entirely to the Agent while humans focus on decisions and security approvals. That is the right way to do AI-assisted development.
